2 McDOU GALL'S Pategt SELF—RAISING FLOUR AIMS Ttm. The Examiner, Saturday, November 24, 1906 WARRINGTON INFIRMARY. DEWSBURY DEPUTATION'S CONCLUSIONS. Which is the More Economically Managed ?

pass muster, but both from an e'conomical and orna- mental point of view, cheap cloths, serges, tweeds, velvets and velveteens are not a success. There is only one way by which the girl or woman blessed with little pocket money can hope to present a smart appearance to the world, and that is by making her clothes herself. We are most of us aware that the utter hopelessnees of trying to find a cheap dressmaker, who can turn out articles of attire fit to he seen, but for a few pence very excellent patterns lie ready to our hand, full length dress stands cost comparatively little, moreover a machine of some sort or other finds a place in every home, and the best thing is to set to work with a deter- minotion to do better ourselves. The wise plan for the amateur to follow is to begin on underskirts, then advance to skirts; to commence on slips and then go on to blouses, It is little short of wonderful how quickly the average girl can " pick up " dressmaking if she sets herself to work in earnest, and the sum charged by the cheap dressmaker for making, or rather spoiling a gown will more often than not cover the cost of a dress-length of good material. Forthcoming Styles.—There are again rumours to the effect that tunics, double skirts, and draperies will be worn as winter advances, but so far these styles are little seen. Skirts are either lightly fitting over the hips, and flowing out from thence to the hem, or gathered into the waist all round, and at present there seems little likelihood of any change. The Princess gown is still enjoying an immense vogue, and velvet princess evening gowns are in high favour among leading dressmakers. Not too Tall, and very Slim.—An absorbing idea of the moment is to appear as slim RS possible, therefore striped materials, and textures invested with vertical predominate. The waist too is placed as high as it can be, an impossible vogue for the very tall. At the present time the slim woman of moderate inches is having things all her own way in the modistie world, but she must not run away with the notion that this state of things will go on indefinitely. MAD GE.

It will be remembered that a short time ago a depute- Lion from the Board of Management of the Dewsbury Infirmary visited the Warrington Infirmary with the object of ascertaining whether their own institution could be worked more economically. At a recent meeting of the Dewsbury Infirmary Board the conclu- sions of the deputation were announced and they will, we think, be read with interest by Warringtonians. It was reported that the House Committee, after spending some considerable time in going through the comparative statement of account of Dewsbury and Warrington, passed the following resolution :—" The House Committee, after visiting the Warrington Infir- mary, and carefully comparing the cost of working the same against that of Dewsbury, are fully satisfied that for efficient and economical management, the balance of 'evidence is in favour of onr own insnitution," In proposing the adoption of the minutes, Mr. E. 'Fitton refered at some length to the resolution with reference to the visit to Warrington. He said that the committee desired to see if they could economise or improve the working of the Infirmary by compaiison with other institutions, and, finding that Warrington stood out prominently in the matter of economy, they paid them a visit. They 4k-ere cordially received by the members of the House 'Committee, who were ready to supply, all the information they could. It appeared they had an endowment fund of £26,000, and he wished their institution had a similar amount to its credit. Four persons comprised the House and Finance Committees, so that in the matter of representation, Dewsbury was better served. They had two doctors— as against Dewsbury's one—but the staff and the work- ing arrangements, generally, were remarkably like Dewsbury's. They had the same number of domestics, but Dewsbury had one more nurse. The staff holidays were very similar, but Warrington had no diet list, which helped to cheapen the working expenses. The maintenance of an in patient cost £5B 158. per annum at Warrington, and Dewsbury's cost on the same basis was £55 18s. He did not wish them to think he was trying to make figures prove anything. The only motive the House Committee had was to learn something to their advantage. With regard to therworking generally, it appeared that last year Warrington treated 2,700 more cases than Dewsbury, but they were mostly out-patients and casualties. On the comparative scale for the past ten years, it would have cost Dewsbury £ll5 more to treat those cases. Whilst Warrington had two doctors to keep, Dewsbury had one more patient and one more nurse to keep, and' they provided food for the char- woman and two porters ; so that those items would cover the difference. In the X-rays departments, War- rington had treated 10 cases, representing 359 exposures, whilst Dewsbury bad treated 27 cases, repre- senting 1,180 exposures ; and the operations at Dewsbury had been considerably more than at Warrington, though at the latter .place, the outside and casualty work was larger. The salaries were also considerably more. Dewsbury's coal, water, and gas bill for 1905 was £5 more than Warrington's, though Warrington's rates and taxes were £56, against Dews.. bury's .E 23. It was difficult, however, to probe to the bottom of things in Warrington's case, as no details were given in the reports, as was the case with Dews- bury's ; so that that they might learn from Dewsbury in the matter of book-keeping. Dewsbury last year had to pay £5O for bank interest, which was a debit War- rington did not incur. Further, in Dewsbury's case,the cost of advertising, postage, and stationery, was much larger, though that was accounted for by the expenses incurred in connection with the Hospital Saturday Fund. Finally, Mr. Fitton thought the board and public might feel perfectly satisfied that the House Committee were doing all they could to work the institution economically, consistent with efficiency ; and taking things all round, they came back from Warrington better satisfied with their own infirmary ; and`for light- ness, brightness and comfort generally, the Dewsbury Infirmary could not be beaten. (Applause). Mr. H. Thorp, after referring to one or two points in Mr. Fitton's remarks, went on to say that at Warring- ton they had not behind them such a noble army of working men as Dewsbury had. He seconded the adoption of the minutes. The Chairman was glad the House Committee had taken such pains to put matters right. There was an impression abroad that compared with Warrington they were extravagant ; but there was a material difference between extravagance and efficiency. He thought the House Committee were deserving of the Board's best thanks. Mr. Yates thought a few words from him would not be out of place, seeing that he was chiefly responsible for the committees visit. From the exhaus- tive report which had been given it would appear that the committee's investigations had been thorough, and he thought the visit would also be of advantage to the authori- ties at Warrington which was his native place. With respect to what Mr. Thorp had said, they had an army of workers for the Dewsbury Infirmary, noble not only in numbers, but noble also in their strength of affection for the institution. He thought that it was perfectly clear from the report that that institution was conducted no the right lines. Mr. Fitton said he would like to add that Warrington took in private patients at a guinea a week, and domestic servants at 103. The Board of Guardians sub- scribed ten guineas per annum to the infirmary, and the Corporation subscribed fifteen guineas per annum. They charged a pehny for every bottle of medicine, powder, or dressing issued from the dispenary, and in that way raised £3 or £4 a week. The minutes were then adopted,

was stretched out for the photograph—the photo- graph beside which a vase of fresh flowers always stood. He took hold of it, turzed it, looked at it; then the eyes of the two men challenged, blazed at one another. "You are the man!" Dick said, his voice scarcely above a whisper. "Yes," John answered. "1 am the man ! " "You think you are going to marry her ?" "No, I know lam going to marry her. Listen to me, Dick." He moved nearer to his brother. "I have always loved her; she has always, since her early girlhood, been dearer to me than any- one else in the world. My heart always hungered and thirsted for her, but you won her, and so as far as possible I locked my passion in my breast. I was absolutely loyal to you, my brother; the news of your death gave me the right to woo her, win her, and to-morrow she will be my wife." 5".120-morrow ?" /"To-morrow." The younger man laughto. "I am home, then, in the nick of time," he said. "I am sorry for you, Jack, genuinely sorry, but only one man can win, and mine is the prior claim. II am the man she loves; I dare swear though she has given her consent to become your wife, she has never given you her love. Things being as they are, late as it is,e I must let her know the truth to-night; she shan't wake to-morrow thinking the day will make her your wife." He took a step towards the window. . . .

"Yes," he answered, "the same time as usual. r suppose all the packing is done?" "Yes, sir." "And your own ?" "Thank you, yes, sir." "Then you can go off to bed. Good-night." "Good-night, sir. I—you've hurt your hand, ir. "

John moved liackwards, barring his exit. "You will not go to her," he said, "either to-night or to-morrow; you will not interfere with her, unsettle her. Whether she loves me or no is my concern, and mine alone. Any way, she is almost mine bone of my bone, flesh of my flesh, no man shall rob me of her nOw—least of, all the man who could make her suffer as she has suffered. You could stay away a year, enjoying yourself in your own way, I'll be bound. You can go away for another, or as many more as you like. and—l don't expect a concession for nothing—you can go away with plenty of money in your pocket. I will give you almost anything you like to ask, but you shall not—you shall not snatch My joy from me! I "—he spoke the words so calmly it made them seem doubly terrible— "would kill you first A" Dick started ever so slightly, then once more he laughed. "Oh, don't talk,rot! Bhe said. "This isn't • melodrama. I tell you I'm sorry for you—l don't see that I can say more—but I'm certainly not going to stand aside while you marry the woman who loves me, whom I love. Any way—yes, I'll be perfectly fair— she shall choose between us. If she prefers you, to-morrow's wedding must go on, I suppose. If she prefers me, we will fix an early date, and you must look out for another girl—goodness .knows there are enough in the world! Come, .Isck, let's be sensible over this affair—let c' 'ia arbitrate between us. I'll "—he looked av .11 at the clock —"leave it until to-morrow, if you wish. After all, it's rather late to knock the poor little girl up. I wish you'd ring for brandy-and-soda, I'm confoundedly thirsty. He sank into a chair as he spoke aa irritating smile on his face. He took up the photograph again, looked at it, raised it to his lips, kissed it. "Little darling! " he said. "I believe you're prettier than ever, or is it that I haven't seen anyone half so lovely sinoe I've been away? shall I ring, Jack?" He glanced from the photograph to his brother. The man's expression was absolutely furious.

"How dare you!" he said. "Put down that photograph." Dick shrugged his shoulders. "Oh, all right," he answered, "I don't know that I'm particularly keen on kissing cardboard, and within twelve hours I shall kiss the original. Don't look so savage, Jack, I'm not trying to rile you; you must see the game, so far As you are concerned, is up. Do, for Heaven's sake, ring the bell, or permit me." He half-rose, then, as John moved, sat down again. Crossing. to the bell, the elder brother had to pass behind the other; as he did so once more Dick took up the photograph. Whetlmr that was the last straw, or whether the idea had already come into John Brandon's mind, it would be difficult to say. Any way, the action made, for a moment, a madman of him; he caught up a heavy ruler, and with all his strength brought it down upon his brother's head, stunning him instantly, and even then, time after time, with a dull thud, the ruler fell and fell.

The utter absence of anything approaching retaliation sobered John Brandon. Even a wild beast will not harm a creature that is motionless, but, crouching down, will wait patiently for any movement. With a slight shiver John Brandon laid the ruler on the table.

"I'm sorry," he said, half aloud, "but I've stopped your interfering with to - morrow's ceremony; by the time you come to yourself, we shall be man and wife, and nothing—nothing but death will part us." Probably he did not realise how savagely he had used the ruler • certainly he only believed the man to be stunned. With some difficulty he lifted him from the chair and laid him on the sofa. When he came to, he could get him up to bed, tell the servants Mr. Dick had come home ill, give orders to his man to look after him, and go off to his own wedding. The head of the unconscious man dropped back unpleasantly; his eyes were fixed; his mouth half opened, as though a cry had almost escaped it; a little blood trickled down his white face. John wiped it away quite tenderly. "I'm awfully sorry," he said, still speaking aloud, "but, by Heaven! I could not loose her!' He sat down, waiting to hear the servants shutting up; his man would come to him for any last orders, he knew; he would meet him at the door, from which the sofa could not be seen. Then he would restore his brother to consciousness..

-------- - Every now and then the guns from the Convict Prison still boomed out, and did not tend to enliven matters. John Brandon sat down and watched his brother. The servants seemed late In locking up. The unconscious man never moved; so motion- less he lay that at length John Brandon grew uncomfortable.. Dick looked almost like a dead man.

John rose quickly, went to the sofa, and touched his brother's hand; it was colder than It had been—much colder. His eyes stared horribly, his mouth had dropped. "Good Heavens!" John Brandon maid, "I have killed him. How horrible!" He looked round terrified—he was a murderer! He had done his brother to death—the brand of Cain was upon him! And to-morrow was his wedding-day!
Fora Minute fear had paralysed him—that thought braced him to action. His brother was dead—he had killed him; it was no time for remorse—he must hide the body. But where?

He looked round the room; the door was unlocked, the servants about. Any moment his man might come to him. His eyes fell on the great safe let into the wall. A man could have stood upright in it; there was a hiding-place for the time being, at all events. He flung open the door, crossed to the sofa, took up the body, carried it with, difficulty across the room, lowered it gently within the safe, shut and locked the door.
As he did so, some slight sound outside startled him; he looked towards the window, the blind was down. "The wind," he said to himself; /that was all —the wind."

He sat down, took up the photograph of the girl he loved, kissed it tenderly; all the horrible rage that had so transfigured the expression of his face left it; there was nothing but tenderness, love and serenity there. With the shutting of the door of the safe, he seemed to have forgotten his.brother'and the horror that had happened. He heard footsteps in the hall, bolts being shot; the booming of the guns went on. Then his man entered the room, a silver tray, with light refreshments on it, in his hand. "Is there anything more, sir, to-night ? " he asked. "Nothing," John answered. "You can go to bed, I shan't want you. You've heard the guns, of course ?" "Yes, sir," the man answered; "a convict's escaped, I suppose. Poor fellow! Little enough, good it will do him, they will have him before morning." "Probably," John Brandon answered. "Pay particular attention to the locks and bolts, Robert, he might possibly make for this house— we don't want him harbouring here—and lock every room door, as well as bolting and barring , the windows."

"Very good, sir, he answered. "Shall I call you at the usual time, sir ? " Hereto John Brandon had kept the keys of the safe in his hand. Now, hardly thinking what he was doing—his thoughts all with Celia—he opened a drawer of his writing-table, and threw tham in.

John Brandon looked down, there was blood upon it, and he had not noticed—his brother's blood! His face blanched to the whiteness of paper. "It's nothing," he said, quickly, "only a scratch. You need not wait." The man went from the room, not giving another thought to .the blood on his master's hand. John Brandon shivered as he wiped it off; it was almost dry, and troublesome to remove. He threw the handkerchief he had used from him in horror, then he poured himself out liberal supply of whisky, filled the class up with soda-water, and drank it off. He felt better at once; the spirits quieted his nerves, which the sight of blood on his hands had upset. He rose to his feet. "I'll be off to bed," he said, half aloud. "The sooner I am asleep the better, for more reasons than one. The chief reason, little lady "—he looked at the photograph of Celia—"because time passes very quickly while we are asleep, and waking I shall be very near the hour of my wedding, sweetheart." He switched off the light, and went from the room, closing and locking the door after him. It was Almost phenomenal but he had put the death I of his brother out of his mind, or perhaps it was !that his thought was so occupied with the woman he loved tbat there was no room for any other. ,I He went to his room. The lights were up • it Pooked warm and cosy, though it was furnished with some severity, and an utter absence of lace or silk or satin. It was the last time he would occupy it. A suite of rooms had been most luxuriously furnished for him and his bride when they should return from their honeymoon. He looked round and laughed to himself, he could not quite have told why; then, with a sudden impulse, he left his room, and passed down the corridor to the suite of rooms lately re- furnished. The door was locked. He turned the key and entered, switching on the, light as he 'I went from room to room. All were beautiful, all were luxurious. He drew a deep breath as he looked around him. the colour came to his cheeks, his eyes shone. These were the rooms to be occupied by his wife and himself after their return from the honeymoon. There seemed something sacred about them to him. He walked softly, almost noiselessly, touching drapery or hangings here and there with loving fingers. Already she had walked through the rooms with him, had approved everything, had praised his taste kindly, if not enthusiastically. In a month's lime she would be quite, quite at home there—his bride, his wife! He sat down on a couch and thought of the morning. All remembrance of his brother, of the tragedy, had left him. It was very curious, but it was so. To-morrow would give him Celia, to he his very own. He loved her most passion- ately, most tenderly. In time she would love him. Good women he had heard, always loved their husbands; and she was perfect. He rose after a time. With one more look round he switched off the lights. "I suppose I must get to bed," he said to him- self. "I could sit and thikk here all night, hut--"

His thoughts came to an abrupt conclusion. Someone was knocking loudly at the front door— loudly and persistently Even then, he gave no thought to his dead brother. He wondered what the knocking could mean. He hurried downstairs. He heard distant doors open; some of the menservants, half- dressed, hurried down. John Brandon was first in the hall. He drew back the bolts, unfastened the chain, and opened the door. The brilliant light from the hall fell upon the faces of a number of prison warders. John Brandon knew at once the reason of their coming. One of the men stepped forward. "Very sorry to disturb you, sir," he said. ."You've heard the guns' of course? One of the prisoners has escaped. We've traced him here; we're almost sure he has got into the house. You'll be just as anxious as we are, I'm- sure, to have it searched. May we come ? 7 John moved back d little. "Certainly," he i answered, "but it's hardly likely, I think, that the man is here. All the doors and windows are fas tened. " "Which means just nothing to Tom Thorny- croft—No. 27, as we knew him. None but a genius could have escaped as he has. But he's in here, we're pretty certain, Mr. Brandon, and we'll find him if we have to search every nook and corner, every hole that a mouse could hide in. We won't be long, sir; we've run our quarry to earth, I'm pretty sure of that:" The men entered the house as the chief warder spoke. John Brandon looked at the menservants. "It's hardly likely anyone can have gained .entrance here, is it?" he asked. • "Next door to impossible. I should 'say, sir,* one of them answered. "We'd heard the guns. We were more particular than usual. Besides, it he's a clever fellow, he'd have been too 'cute to take refuge in a house, like a rabbit in a burrow; he'd have been sure of being turned out and caught. If he's come this way, he's much more likely dodging round some of the outhouses." The qief warder looked at John Brandon. "It's ahnost certain that he's here," he said. "We all but had our hands on him once to night. We went so close to him that we heard him steal away. I know very well what his game is. • He's not the sort to stick about in hiding for days; he'll make a bolder shot for freedom. But he got to get rid of his convict dress, and to do that he must steal other clothing. If we put a strong cordon round the house, I fancy we shall ferret him out and catch him. Any way, we'll do cur best."
CHAPTER V. "HE WILL WORK ILL TO ME.*

"Not in bed, Miss Celia?" Celia Verde shook her head. "What a ridiculous thing to say! " she answered. "You can see I'm not. can't you ? Do you hear those horrible guns ? Some poor wretch making a dash for freedom. I was just saying my prayers when the first boomed out, and I prayed that he might get safe away." Emily looked shocked. "Oh, Miss Celia, and he may be a murderer!"

_ . "Yes, I know. It was an impulse. I ought not to have done it; but I always feel so sorry for them. It's natural they should try to get away. It's horrible they should be hunted with guns like wild beasts. Of course I know some of them are worse than wild beasts, and yet--" she leant her cheek upon her pretty hand. "I am I sorry I did what I did—l suppose my nerves are . rather to pieces to night; but directly the prayer wat3 prayed, I felt it would be answered, that the man would get safely away, that in the future he would work ill to me and mine. I felt quite I frightened—that's why I sent for you." Lady Caroline's maid was in her dressing- gown. She had been in bed when her young mistress's bell had rung, but not asleep. She still trembled at the remembrance of the ghost I she had seen. She still looked pale and afraid. "I'm glad you did ring, miss," she said, "but you ought to be in bed. You ought to get a good night's rest so as to look your very best to. Morrow. Do you know what time it is ?" Celia looked round at the clock. It was past twelve. "I haven't been thinking of the time she answered, "and I don't want to go to bed. Directly I am asleep it will be to-morrow-- or so it will seem to me—and I don't know that I want to-morrow hero—to-morrow that is to change my life. You won't understand that, ! Emily, r daxesay. You've most likely got a! young man. You think it's very delightful to be with him. You love your Sunday out, but you'vo I never yet stood, as it were, upon the threshold ,of married life. I think that must make any girl I a little afraid. One stands at the portals of ' , the unknown, and the unknown is to be entered-- until death us do part." Emily looked more than interested. "But if ! you love him, Miss Celia, it seems to me you'd feel quite safe even in taking an unknown journey." "But suppose you don't?" Celia answered. I "You know, Emily, was engaged before. I was going to marry Mr. Brandon's brother. Everyone tells me he was not so satisfactory as my hus- band of toorrbw, but I loved him better. I! think had been going to marry him I should have said to the hours that separated us, ' hurry, hurry ! ' whereas now lam saying, lag, lag! I am holding them back with all my might, ' perhaps because I've such a queer feeling all ilay long that Dick Brandon is near me. He can't be, of course, because he is dead—dead and buried in far-off Africa. But perhaps .(

div.head: WRITTEN IN SCARLET.
div.p: WRITTEN IN SCARLET.
BY ALICE MAUD MEADOWS, author of "One Life Between," "A Million of Money," "The Extreme Penalty," "For Levi of a Lady," "I Charge You Both,' &a.

SYNOPSIS OF Pitt/CEDING CHAPTERS: It is the wedding eve of John Brandon, a well-to-do country gentleman, and Celia Verde, daughter ,of Lady Caroline Verde. Celia had been engaged to John's . brother Dick, a wild and reckless young man, supposed to have died abroad. Celia admits that she loved her old sweetheart better than the nevi— in fact, that she does not love John at all. He, , however, adoring her, promises himself that he Will ! win her love after marriage. Then all is changed by the sudden reappearance of Dick, who meets his brother as he is going homewards. No other person has seen the wanderer except Lady Caroline's maid, who takes him for a ghost.

CHAPTER IV. PRISON GUNS. Against the blustering wind, through the moist, heavy air, the darkness of a moonless night, the two men walked side by aide, neither for a time speaking, both very busy with their thoughts. The long grass and bracken switched damp and dank against their feet; wild animals skuddied out of their pathway; a bird flew up close to them, striking their faces with its wings. Not a soul seemed about. The two men had the World to themselves, both thinking their thoughts, which were with one woman the thoughts of one carelessly tender, of the other passion- ately jealous. Heart, body, and soul, with every throb and thrill of his nature, he loved her; and this man—this brother of his who had left her without a word for more than a year—had come back to claim her! In spite of the darkness the red, horrible mist of blood was before his eyes; his hands clenched and clenched, whilo his heart cried, "No, no, not that! My brother—my only brother ! " .Dick whistled a few bars of a comic song as th.-iy trudged along, then broke off suddenly. "What's eome to you, Jack ? " he said. "Don't you want to know what I've been Up to all this long time? Aren't you curious? I suppose you're in a paddy because I've caused you a certain amount of anxiety. I realise that is natural, of course. For all that, one would have thought the joy of seeing me again would overcome the resentment, or whatever you like to call it. You're not exactly killing the fatted calf in cordiality, are you ? Well, old chap "—he I slipped his arm through his brother's—"it's not altogether my fault. I did almost peg out, had more than one leg over the border-line, when some clever Johnnie of a doctor pulled me back. I might have written then, of course, but I thought I'd like to surprise you. I can see it was a rotten idea, and perhaps I've caused you all unnecessary suffering. Still, one and all, you , can dry your eyes now and rejoice. I say, Jack, , tell me something about Celia. How did she take the news of my death ? Hard, I'll be , bound, little darling! ' One could tell from the tone of his voice that he was smiling, beaming with conceit, with gratified vanity; that the woman he had pro- fessed to love, professed still t ) love, had suffered because of him was incense to his self- esteem. John's hands clenched. "You made her suffer, if that's any comfort to you," he answered. "You took the light from her eyes the glow from her cheeks. For a time you checked the joy, the happiness of her life, but you did not kill it. You '—he drew himself up, he laughed with the strange, hard laughter of passion—"are not the only man in the world. There are others; there is another." The younger man came to an abrupt stop. "Another ?" he repeated. "What do you mein, another lover ? ' "Another lover," John went on; "a better man than you, a man who really loves her—her the woman, not the pretty face, the outward semblance. A man who will guard her, cherish her, keep all grief from her; a man who would rather die than give her one moment's pain. You talk about loving her, and you have left her for over a year. Love! You don't know the mean- ing of the word. You love yourself, your pleasure, the gratification of your whims, your vanity. As for anything else, it is a rialed book to you." He had not paused. Catching him up, the younger man again kept .pace with him. The joy went out of his heart, some- thing seemed to tighten round it. Once more he caught John Brandon's arm. "Who is the man," he said "this lover, this

Simon pure, this good and virtuous man? Ah, well "—his grasp relaxed—"it matters very little. I don't care; she tolerated him because she had mourned me dead; things will be different when she sees inc again, when I take her in my arms once more, kiss her, claim her. Still, I'm a trifle curious. Who is the man ?" John Brandon did not speak. They were near- ing the house now, • walking across the velvet- soft lawn that had been cut and rolled, and cut and rolled for centuries. The persistent wind had at length swept the clouds away. A new moon, like a sickle of silver, minus its handle, shone feebly from the dark sky. A hare sitting motionless almost in the path of the two men, watched them pass without moving. To race off might mean to attract attention, and how was he to know their profession was not that of the poacher ? The heart of each man was beating quickly. Angrily Dick repeated his question. "Who is this man—this fool, who thinks for a moment he can step into my shoes ? " John Brandon looked upward at the crescent moon. Light, as everyone knows, is the greatest, the deadliest enemy of evil. Darkness and deeds that are dark rub shoulders nine times out of ten. There would, perhaps, have been a crime committed then and there, but for the gentle rays of Luna. "I will tell you,'" John Brandon answered. "Don't—don't make a mistake, you have lost her, as you deserved to lose her, and those who love her thank Heaven for it. You are not the ' man to make a woman happy. The library window is open, come in that way. The servants would be frightened did they see you before I had explained. We all thought--" Ho paused abruptly. A loud report startled the silence of the night, echoing and reverberat- ing all around, then another and another. "The guns from Dartmoor," Dick said. "A prisoner has escaped. Poor wretch! I wonder will his friends be as glad to see him back from a living death as you appeared to be to see me, as yoethought, from the tomb?" John did not answer. Again and again the guns boomed forth. He put his hand on the frame of the French window, pushed it, and entered, not a soul seeing them. Then he switched on the electric light, closed the window, and drew down the blinds. , In the brilliant white light, both men looked , haggard, both were pale. The face of the younger . man was the handsomer, but it was not altogether , a satisfactory countenance. The handsome eyes i were too near together; the beautiful mouth : was weak. A phrenologist would have dubbed him fickle, insincere at once; and yet, while any fancy lasted, Dick was enthusiastic enough about it. The pity was, no fancy lasted very long. ! Again and again the guns boomed out. Dick glanced round his brother's study; nothing seemed much altered in the year during which he had been absent. There were more books in . the great bookcase, perhaps; the Turkey • carpet was new; the great safe let into the wall had had a fresh coat of paint; the leather chairs had had a new maroon covering. The writing-table, strewn with papers, stood in its accustomed place. There seemed but two innovations—a theva s e picture f tl'.l; errnse adntdo towards aprldt photograph. t Dick,og rap he. sTeh ob awc where e or ef John's pen lay. Dick noticed it, but felt no curiosity; he was thinking of his own affairs and of Celia. ! "Who is the man ?" he said for the third time. "You may as well tell inc. If you do not I shall find out first thing to-morrow. I shall go to her—she'll be glad enough to see me—and I shall say to her: ' You have entered into this ! engagement supposing line to be dead. You are still my affianced wife. I have come home to marry you,' and she will be glad, with all her heart and soul. All you say about inc may or . may not be true; any way, it's beside the mark, since she loves me, and I am back here again. ! Who is this poor fellow, who must learn the truth of the old adage, Twixt cup and lip there's many a slip '? " ! He moved towards the table as he spoke; why, he could hardly have said. John watched him, not uttering a word. Had a suspicion of the • truth entered Dick's mind? Perhaps. His hand

A Naval Career for the Princes.—lt has been decided that the young Princes of Wales are to enter next Easter at the Royal Naval College, Osborne, and they will probably find that British lads are not great respecters of persons, at any rate with regard to those Who are doing the same work as they are themselves engaged in. Commander Statham tells us in his "History of the Brittannia "that the Prince of Wales and Prince Albert Victor, were allotted separate quarters, put apart from that their life was very much I the same as that of other cadets, who plied them with such questions as "How do you like being a Prince?' "What do you do when you are at home?" and "Do I you ever get licked?" There is nothing very original or brilliant in these interrogations, and it must he admitted that they are less striking than the super- scription of a note which a tutor at Eton intercepted as it was being passed to the Duke of Albany—now the Duke of Saxefboburg-Gotha. The epistle was addressed to " His Royal Foolishness. dirty-faced Albany." Another Gilbert and Sullivan Revival.—The play- going world is shortly to see a revival of the Gilbert and Sullivan operas, a revival coinciding with the entry of the famous librettist on his seventy-first year. It was in 1896 that Mr. W. S. Gilbert first caine out as a dramatic author, and he has produced more plays than than the number of his years, but it was the dozen or so of the Savoy operas the result of his partnership with Sir Arthur Suillivan,which proved such striking thematic successes, and made his name immortal. Some of the most famous of these Savoy operas are to be given again in London and there is little doubt that the revival will be heartily welcomed by the playgoing public. Attracting a Congregation.—The Rev. C. H. Grundy has remarkeoiothat if a clergyman were an eloquent preacher, a good and scholarly man, and were at the same time an expert performer upon the tin whistle, he would be known, not as a preacher, a scholar, or even as a good man, but as the clergyman who played a tin whistle. The minister of a Baptist Church in New York, who must be in some respects a good deal unlike his brethren on this side of the Atlantic seems to have placed himself in a similarly dangerous position. •Find- ing that people had removed from the neighbourhood of his church, and that he was left with a very spare con- gregation, he conceived the idea of enlisting the help of a whistling lady, well-known in the halls. The experiment was in one way successful, for the church was crowded. The pastor's view probably is that so long as the people remain outsiderhe can do nothing with them, and no doubt he made the best of his oppor- tunity when he had the congregation before him, but however much the experiment may be successful in drawing people to church, there is something repugnant to British ideas in introducing a music hall turn " to a place of worship, and it is sate to say that the example is not likely to be followed in this country. The Registrar and Christian Names.—An aggrieved parent who withed to name his little daughter" Coralie" seems justified in his complaint of the Registrar who refused it on the score that there was no such name. Now and again parents are found who wish to give their children such ill-chosen or even spiteful names, that the registrars have discretionary powers to refuse them, but it is difficult to see what objection could be taken to " Coralie." It may be uncommon, but is found occasionally among Christian names. The parents, however, can easily have it restored, as the name of a child registered in this way can be altered at any time within twelve months, but if named in baptism it is a much more difficult matter to have it rectified. Naming the Baby.—Mr. J. H. Settle has come to the assistance of those parents who are perplexed over finding names for their offspring. He has written a book Names for Baby " which gives a selection of all possible Christian names, with their derivation and supposed meanings. In the old days one Christian name sufficed for one person, but in the Victorian age, two became common, and now is is not unusual to have three or more, generally of an aristocratic or high- sounding tone, so that Mr. Settle may be said to have supplied "a long left want " in providing us with ready facilities for their selection. Many old families retain old-fashioned names. In the ducal house of Somerset there is always a Jane. In the Marlborough family the sacred name is Sarah and in the Hamiltons, Anne, and so on but as a general rule where old-fashioned names are retained they are relegated to the second or third place. Names that date a woman from a war, a corona- tion, or other public event, are of course a mistake, as are also those commencing with a vowel, or the letter "h "as in that event the owners are condemned to hear a good deal more of the misuse of the aspirate than they otherwise would. Cale should always be taken , that initials do not spell an unfortunate word, ftS in the case of the late Sir Arthur Seymour Sullivan, the famous composer, whose initials were A. S. S. The Home Dressmaker.—There is no douht whatever that to the woman posseszed of a small dress allowance the winter is the most trying season in the year. First and foremost, of course, she feels the need of good furs, and then winter fabrics are very much more expensive than summer ones. Cheap airy-fairy materials may

Soreness and swelling in the knees—as in housemaid's knee—is commonly the result of too much kneeling. A Hull case shows that serious ulcers may develop if proper care is not taken and points to the wisdom of rubbing in Zarn-Buk occasionally upon any surface of skin that is liable to soreness or excessive strain. Miss Edith Carr Forth, of 3, Tigar-lane, North Bar- street, Beverley, told a local reporter :—" My knees got bruised and sore through hard work in a country house. Then they began to swell, and the dye from my stockings seemed to get in. Large holes appeared in the flesh, and one of my knees grew to the size of my head. I was compelled to leave my situation and go home. The joints were poulticed, but the swelling increased, and when the scabs came away the discharge was awful. A doctor's ointments didn't seem to have any effect. "I had thirty poultices on in one day, and on several occasions the discharge was most alarming. Seven running wounds had formed, the smallest being as big as a sixpence. They were always inflamed and painful, and nci tongue can tell the agony I suffered. I got so weak that I never expected to leave my bed alive. -

"For about sixteen weeks I was treated as an out- patient at the infirmary, and then it was suggested that I should undergo an operation. They said this was the only cure, but just then I read about Zam-Brik, and decided it should be given a trial. My knee was just at its worst when the first dressing of Zam-Buk was put on, yet the pain was'soon eased and the inflammation gradu- ally died down. We persevered with Zam-Buk, and could point to some improvement every day. The swelling decreased very quickly, the discharge ceased, and soon my legs were of normal size. When we had been using Zare-Buk a week or two I found that I could walk quite well without the bandages. One by one the the wounds closed up,and were covered with new,sound skin. Altogether I used about a dozen boxes of Zam-Buk, and I can truthfully shy that this excellent balm alone cured me. I have been quite well now for nearly three months."

New Bankruptcy Proceedings published in the London Gazette, 101; Deeds of Arrangement registered,77. making his poor spirit diSquieted. That would be horrible, would it not? And yet he can't expect, can he, that I should lead a lonely life ?" Emily's face had blanched to even greater whiteness. She would have given anything almost—certainly everything of which she was possessed—to have told the girl what she had seen, but she had promised Lady Caroline ta keep silent, and she kept her word. "He can't indeed," Emily answered, and could not keep a tremble out of her voice. "It's natural though, I think, that your thoughts should turn to him to-night. Would you like me to stay with you, Miss Celia ? I will if you. •like, but you really ought to get to bed." Once more the guns from the prison broke the silence of the night. "It's horrible to hear them, isn't it ?" iCelia said. "Do they seem to say anything to you? They do to me. and I think they must to the escaping man. Every time they break the silence I seem to hear the words—Search, search! Yes, stop With me if you will. As you say, I'd better go to sleep; though my looks to-morrow really don't matter; the newspapers, probably, have written their account of the ceremony already, and have said. that I looked beautiful. Mr. Brandon would think me charming even had I been crying my eyes out. Beauty is in the eyes of the beholder, and hits eyes have photographed upon them a presentment of me that is absolutely perfect. 12;otir Jack! " She was asleep very soon after her pretty head was laid ,upon the pillow. Not so Emily; she wrapped herself up in a thick rug, and lay down on the sofa. An incandescent light in the room burnt feebly, but as the hours went on, it seemed to grow brighter and brighter, until the room was quite light. Emily could not sleep; do what she would her thoughts would turn to the vision, the apparition she had seen. "Rest, rest, perturbed spirit! " she said, softly, with a vague remembrance of Shakespeare. "What good would it do to you if she did remain unmarried? She could he nothing to you—a spirit. Take your flight elsewhere, don't appear before me again, and if you love her, don't— :don't appear before her. You half frightened me out of my life—you would kill her outright!" (To be continued.)

WIDNES RANGERS V. WARRINGTON "A."—Played at Widnes on Saturday in stormy weather. The visitors won the toss, and in the first half played with the wind in their favour. The Rangers were kept on the defence, and Landor arid Wilson scored tries in quick succession. Both goal kicks failed. Later ii'oster and Jones also got over, no goals resulting. Interval : Warrington " A," 12 points; Widnes Rangers, nil. In the next half, with the wind against them, Warrington had all their own way, but for a long time were unable to improve their position. The Warrington forwards, headed by Swift, came away with a rush, but Doyle kicked in touch. A race for the ball between Cart- wright and Doyle ended in the former scoring a good try in front of the posts. The kick at goal failed. Result : Warrington " A," 15 points; Widnes Rangers, nil.

If there is a characteristic that is above all others to be desired, writes " Ambrosia " in the !World, it is undoubtedly tact, and nowadays it is more than ever necessary when society is so mixed and privacy of affairs well-nigh impos- sible. It is only by judicious management of , tongue, eyes, and manner that one can save one- self and one's friends in the countless awkward I situations that are everywhere occurring. But while tact is a great gift, some folk ofttimes dis- play strange tactlessness in making it known that they do possess it. People resent being managed, and invariably suspect you if they think you are checking their indiscretion •or saying less than you might if you were not tactful. Tact, to be used successfully, must be used spontaneously, and, I like charity, it must not be puffed up. On the whole, perhaps, modern men and women under- stand it better than their forebears. div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
DRESS VERSUS POLITICS.

Women in China, it is said, excluded from politics, are , finding refuge in dress. Is there not here, perhaps, asks Miranda," an um conscious suggestion for those who are, appa. rently, far from happy in their role of suftra. gette? Now that the ladies in China no longei worry their heads With affairs of State, but plunge deeply into the alluring mysteries oi European dress, an era' -of emancipation hal dawned, and their power is rapidly on the ascen dant. Who can say even that the little Orienta suffragette is not, after all, much more likely tc achieve her ambition in a perfect toilet than b 3 entering into muscular conflict with the Pekit police?

div.head: SCIENCE NOTE'S AND NEWS.
div.p: SCIENCE NOTE'S AND NEWS.
THE VEGETABLE cATERPILLAR.

The so-called vegetable caterpillar of New Zealand is an interesting example of a fungus sprouting out from the body of an animal which it has killed by the ramification of its hyphte. The caterpillar feeds and grows, while the fun- gus develops in its tissues. Finally the cater- pillar is killed, and its body converted into a woody substance. Then there sprouts up from its head a fungus of considerable size which is edible, and eaten by the natives.

div.head: AN ABSOLUTE TEST FOR DEATFI.
div.p: AN ABSOLUTE TEST FOR DEATFI.

In view of the possibility of premature burial, an absolute test of death is greatly to be desired. The Scientific American gives a brief note of what professes to be an infallible criterion. It is a German invention, and con- sists in the injection of fluoreine deeply into the tissues. If circulation exists the skin and mucous membrane turn yellow, and the eyes be- come an emerald green. If death has really taken place this does not happen. The injection should be made at least two hours before the body is placed in the coffin. If life is not ex- tinct the injection does no harm, and the colour passes off quickly.

div.head: BRAIN OF THE NEGRO.
div.p: THE BRAIN OF THE NEGRO.

The differences of the brain and mental traits as fundamental conditions may be the primary cause of everything relating to the race question, other causes being secondary or merely symp- toms resulting from the elemental conditions. If this be true, says a writer in the Century, the remedy should be applied to the brain and mind of the negro. But is the condition hereditary and fixed, or is it due to environment and alter- able? Is it capable of change, or is it stable? Is the negro capable of mental development in the same way as is the Caucasian? Time alone can answer these questions. History, investiga- tions, experiments, and existing conditions indi- cate that traits are hereditary and stable, and that the negro is not capable of mental develop- ment in the same way that the Caucasian is. The remedy should be to develop the negro along the lines of natural inclination and fitness, which lines must be established scientifically, not senti- mentally.

div.head: COAL STORES UNDER WATER.
div.p: COAL STORES UNDER WATER.

According to Mr. E. Seymour Bell, the British Commercial / Agent in the United States, an electric company have adopted the plan of stowing coal under water at their new plant west of Chicago. The company have con- structed twelve pits, the walls of which are made of cement. Each pit, or , bin, is about 80ft. in length and 251 t. wide, with a depth of some 16ft. They lie in one solid block, three in a row counting side by side; or four in a row end to end. The rectangular space occupied is thus about 320 ft. in length by 75ft. in width. Longitudinally the division walls are wide enough for a railway track, two of which thus run lengthwise through the storage yard, so that the coal from the cars can be dumped into the bins beneath on either side. Under these tracks is built a series of arches in the separating walls, eight for each bin, thereby connecting the bins. The separating concrete walls at the ends are about 18in. in width. The bottom of the pits consists of clay soil. A 12in. water pipe opens to the vats near the top, so that the coal can be readily flooded with water when necessary. The tops of the pits rise aout 4ft. above the natural level of the ground. or the purpose of reload,ing the coal, a steam hovel is used. The stora4e capacity of the pits • estimated at 14,000 tons.

div.head: BIRDS AS FLOWER FERTILISERS.
div.p: BIRDS AS FLOWER FERTILISERS.

During the famous voyage of the Beagle Dse- win observeit an interesting fact about the Chilien mocking thrush. He noticed, that is to say, that its crown was frequently stained yel- low. And this yellow colour was found to be . due to the pollen of some plant. Hence it might be perhaps inferred that this bird was a honey eater. Darwin, however, thought it visited the flower for the beetles which it found feeding on the pollen. In any case, however, it would carg pollen from flower to flower, and thus aid ta cross-fertilisation. Many birds frequenting flowers for honey at insects are thus liable to get their heads covered with pollen. And since the ,pollen of different flowers varies in colour a bird may become yel- low-headed, red-headed, blue-headed, &c. This led to a curious mistake, says the Globe, in the case of a New Zealand bird. This bird was a honey-sucker and a haunter of flewers. Now, in the early summer it visited most frequently the flowers of the native flax, and later in the year fed chiefly on the fuchsia. The pollen •of the former is red, and of the latter blue. Hence in the early summer the bird appeared with a red head, and was named the red-headed honey. seeker. But when later in the year it went to the fuchsia its head was stained blue, and it was called the blue-headed .honey-seeker. Thus, for a long time this bird was thought to be two dis- tinct species, and only recently was it found that the red-headed and blue-headed were one and the same, and that the real colour of the head was blackish brown. •

div.head: WHAT . IS COLD?
div.p: WHAT . IS COLD?

From one point of view, wrote Sir Oliver Lodge, cold is a deadly damaging thing, fatal to high organisms, and a thing to be excluded at all costs. Cold—the cold of a Polar night—the cold of liquid air—will inflict loss of limbs by frost bite, will hurt and pain and kill. No one can afford to despise cold if it be sufficiently intense. Yet what is cold? Is it anything? Was it s thing that had to be created and brought into being? No, it is simply the absence of heat. The absence of, all heat whatever would be absolute zero; and down to such a temperature as that (460 deg. below zero Fahrenheit) no experimenter has yet descended even in the laboratory. In such cold as that all activity would cease, and the material Universe would stagnate into oblivion. Why, then, it cold is only the absence of heat, is it so deadly and destructive? Why is it so intense an evil to human beings? The answer plainly is, because they have attained so high a standard of development, because of their 'high organisation, because of the high tervperature at which they normally exist. Cold will not neces- sarily kill the lowly seed, though it will keep it in suspended animation; but any higher or- ganism it will destroy. . . If we ask, why was cold brought into exist- ence? we are really asking nonsense; what we really mean and must mean is, why was heat brought into • existence? You cannot have heat, and degrees of heat, without having...degrees also of cold; one implies the other. You might have a dead level of temperature where everything would be dull and stagnant and inactive, but in a live and active Universe the degree of heat must vary, and so must the degree of cold.

div.head: POWER OF THE WEAK.
div.p: THE POWER OF THE WEAK.

It is an established fact that a mushroom can make its way through a layer of asphalt, for the phenomenon has been studied and the resistance thus overcome has been calculated in mathemati- cal terms. This resistance is great enough, ap- parently, to rush the mushroom completely. 'es, How, then, is ' \t possible for the fungus to over- come it? The explanation. according to the Physikalbrehc , Zeitsrhrilt, may probably foundin the conditions which make it possible for a trivial quantity of energy to determine the course of a mighty mountain glacier. The thickest mass of ice will yield to a. force operat- ing cohtinually, if gently, and in time the hugest glacier is observed to follow the direction of a . very slight presstire. It goes as water goes, only very much slower. The principle seemingly at work in the case of the glacier and the mush- room may be understood by a simple experiment with a cork, a glass vessel, and some lumps of beeswax. Place a common wine or beer cork inside soi ordinary glass which is empty. Take some lumps of cobbler's wax, each the size of a walnut or thereabouts, and drop them in the glass on top of the cork. In a few days it will be ob- served that the pieces of wax have changed their contours and are in a state of more or less cohe- sion. The height of the mass in the glass is lowered. This process continues—a movemertil analogous to that observable in the case of the glacier—and after some time (this experiment re- quires a little patience) the lumps of wax are welded together. and the space beneath the cork at t-,ke_. bottom of the irlnss is Slow teinsis on ...a

trie wax. -rile s.urtace ot use wax at the top tit the glass presents a horizontal surface. The glass and contents are once more laid aside for an interval. In due time it will be noted that the cork has disappeared from sight. In its place the cobbler's wax will alone be visible at . the bottom of the glass. But in another chie period of time the , rim of the cork will emerge at the, surface and only a little more time will be required for the cork to be floating on the top of the wax. .The difference between the weight of the cork and the weight of the amount of wax it displaced sufficed to bring about this surprising result. The fore exerted was of the slightest, but it sufficed. In the case of the mushroom the pressure was exerted by the growth of the fungus It was „extremely slight, but, as in the case of cork and beeswax, it was persistent, and therefore it achieved the seem- ingly physical impossibility of overcoming a weight. that would seem literally to overwhelm it But in experiments witn corx, glass, anct cobbler's wax the nicest patience is essential if a true flemonstration of a little-known physic.) law is to be obtained in a convincing will.

div.head: BURDEN OF BRONCHITIS. Peps Cure that Persistent Cough.
div.p: THE BURDEN OF BRONCHITIS. Peps Cure that Persistent Cough.

Bronchitis is one of those ailments that "live with us." It attacks some people every winter, especially during foggy weather. It probably kills off more old people than any other single disease. Bronchitis is really inflammation of the delicate membrane lining the tubes that carry the pure air into the lungs. The membrane lining these air passages is well supplied with blood vessels, and is extremely sensitive to chill or any sudden change of temperature. There is a rush of blood to tile affected membrane, setting up the heat and redness inseparable from inflammation. A peculiar tickling in the throat is followed by intense nervous irritation in the region of the breast- bone, while increased secretion of the fluid, normally designed by nature to protect and soften the air passages, gives rise to the familiar choking sensation, and the desire to "cough something up." Great exhaustion is often associated with bronchitis, while , among the other symptoms are feverishness, pain, or tightness about the chest, heavy breathing, headache, and loss of appetite. The cause and character of bronchitis being now made clear, it will be seen of what little use must be the swallowing of bottlesful of cough mixtures into the sterna* to cure something that only has to do with an organ so entirely independent and apart. As one little Pep after another dissolves, breathe the fumes in deeply, when the inflamed air-pas- sages will he bathed in their soothing and healing influence. The phlegm is loosened and thrown out with less discomfort, and the painful inflammation and irritstion are allayed. div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.
MEETING OF THE PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE.

The monthly meeting of the Stockton Heath Parochial Committee was held on Tuesday evening at the Hall Cafe. Mr. G. Pilling presided, and there were present—Messrs. F. Warburton, J. W. Bouchier, J. Whitley, T. Williams, F. Pearson, T. R. Westbrook, H. J. Westbrook, S. F. Welsby, J. H. Clarke, W. Mclntyre, G. F. Ashton (clerk), and J. Swinton (surveyor).

div.head: BREAC-H OF THE BYLAWS.
div.p: BREAC-H OF THE BYLAWS.

Mr. Sugars appeared before the Committee on behalf of Mr. Brierley,Alexander-road, to explain why he com- menced to build a stable before submitting plans to the committee and why the same should not be pulled down, they being in contravention to the bylaws. Mr. Sugars said a sketch plan was submitted to the Surveyor, and as was the rule in other towns they com- menced the building before the plan was approved. Mr. Brierley was prepared to enter into an agreement to pull the building down when called upon. Other buildings in Stockton Heath had been erected without plans having been submitted to the committee. It was impossible to comply with the bylaws in every respect. Mr. Clarke remarked that several small complaints had been received regarding this !Bitter, and protests had been made against the building being erected in such a manner. . .
—„-..-.. The Surveyor having read several complaints, the committee agreed to call upon Mr. Brierley to appear before the District Council to show cause why the erection should not he pulled down.

div.head: THI SWING BRIDGE.
div.p: THI SWING BRIDGE.

A letter was read from the Manchester Ship Canal Co. in reply to the committee's complaint regarding the condition of the footpath on the swing bridge. It stated that the resident engineer bad reported that he had been unable to find anything wrong with the footpaths except that water lodged on one or two of the planks, which were slightly hollow, and holes had since been bored through them for the purpose of drainap. (Laughter). Mr. Whitley said he was surprised at anyone writing such a letter. The bridge was a disgrace to the com- pany. It was decided to reply that the company's letter was not satisfactory.

div.p: STREET LIGHTING.

Mr. Bouchier reported that the Warrington Corpora- tion in the event of the Committee deciding to maintain ' and light their own lamps,had intimated that they would charge them for gas at the same rate as private con- sumers. That was not fair. He proceeded to refer to the irregularity with which the lannps in the village were lighted, and enumerated instances where he found several lamps not lighted. Mr. Clark said he was tired of taking note when lamps were not lighted. He mentioned numerous irregulari- ties in the lit hting of the lamps. Mr. T. R. It was decided to forward a complaint on the matter, whilst the Lighting Committee were empowered to appoint a deputation to wait upon the Corporation.

div.head: WARRINGTON REGHABITES.
div.p: WARRINGTON REGHABITES.
Where the Temperance Party is Lacking. '

Warrington Rechabites spent an enjoyable evening on Saturday when the annual gathering in connection with Charity Tent No. 11, was held in the Brick-street Mission. Tbe proceedings opened with a tea to which a large number sat • down. Afterwards a concert was held over which the Rev. F. Vaughan presided. The CFrATRINIAN said hey was glad to know that the temperance cause was being continued in so able a manner and congratulated the Order upon the great success which it bad attained in its branch of the work. The fact that during the year they had opened 343 new tents and increased their membership by 22,690, was to him simply mavel- lous. Proceeding the Rev. F.. Vaughan urged that they must work for total abolition—nothing else ,would satisfy him. He had not, he said, always been a total abstainer and he had the profoundest sympathy for the poor men, women and children who lived in an atmos- phere which must breed a liking for that upon which the curse of God was most manifestly written. How I were they to bring about reform ! By legislation? He ; thought not. As far as he see the drink traffic was being more strongly entrenched, built up and fortified by legislation. Re had arrived at the solemn conviction that the only force which could make towards real temperance was a moral 1 force—a force which would wean men from a love of sin to alove of holiness and truth. The housing problem in Liverpool had proved uplto the hilt that what was needed more than anything else was not sanitary dwell- ings, not beautiful homes but clean hearts, clean minds and a loftier moral tone. As Spurgeon had said" if you put a pig in aparlour it would be a pig still." He believed the temperance party had been sadly lacking in one particular feature. For seven years he had laboured amongst the dock labourers of T.oiverpool and he had been forced to the conclusion that it was the bounden and Moral duty of the temper- ance party to provide attractive temperance houses in

!which men, tired and weary after their heavy toil could find comfort and at least as warm a;', welcome as they could find in the public-house. ‘Vhen they succeeded in reforming a marl the man had still a frightful struggle before him. On the Monday the man set out deter-. mined and fervent and had to pass fifty trap doors to hell on his way to work. He was not going to say anything harsh about the man if he fell but he said God have mercy on the nation which allowed such a state of things—(Applause)—and upon those who might be guilty in some sense in not cultivating a higher moral tone. He had gone into the public houses with the workingmen and into the British workmen pubfic houses and had been ashamed of theaccommodation in the latter when he saw the nice clean public-house and the warm welcome which was given to those who entered. If he was not the man he professed to be he was not sure that he would not go to the more comfortable place of the two. It seemed to him that the temperance party were missing a grand opportunity and he trusted the time would come when by co-operation they would be able to open two or three houses which would stand deflnitely as homes from home and where a man would be made comfortable. (Applause). Bro. C. W. CHURCHILL, High Chief Ruler of the Order, during the course of an interesting address, said he believed in moral suasion, but he believed that it was best to have with moral suasion legal force. They had to deal with two classes of people, those who could govern themselves and keep from strong drink and those who could not, and they knew that the upbringing and the environment were against the great mass of the latter people who flew to strong drink as a sort of alleviation for the terrible conditions under , which they lived. They had been told that they were on the wrong tack and that poverty was the cause of drunkenness as much as drunkenness was the cause of , poverty. He did not deny that poverty was a cause of some drunkenness but he believed that they found few teetotallers in the slums not because poverty led to , drink but because the total abstainer, however poor, would not live under such conditions. Let them thrust the evil from the land and they would soon be rid of their poverty and their slums. (Applause.) During the evening songs were effectively given by the Misses Woodland and Mr. J. Willett, whilst Bro. E. Sutton, delighted the audience with his humorous recitations in the Lancashire dialect.

div.head: PULPIT ROMANCING.
div.p: PULPIT ROMANCING.
A Vicar's Indictment of the Worldly Church.
THREE DEVILS WHICH AFFLICT CHOIRS.

The Rev. A. M. Mitchell, vicar of Burtonwood,makes i some very sharp criticisms n his !wish magazine about the present day methods of" running "churches, "It has become the fashion, more or less," he says, "to run churches as we run the music or the concert hall. The chief considerations which influence us most are chiefly, 'whatever we do we must please the world,' and the show must pay.' "Pulpit romancing, choir concerts, stage perform- ances, may attract and please the worldling, but do not attract and please the devout worshipper.The success of a church is not to be measured by the popularity of its preaching,nor by the beauty of its musm,nor, yet again, Iby the magnificence of its altar, and " the glorious apparel " of its ministers, - •

div.head: NOVELTIES 'IN PREACHING.
div.p: NOVELTIES 'IN PREACHING.

" Anything to attract, anything to draw ! The latest novelty in preaching humorous and funny discourses, object lessons in the pulpit, brass and other bands in the chancel, are all a matter of business to the minister of worldy motive. "If people are attracted or drawn to advertising churches to have their musical ears tickled by Garnett in D, Goss in A, Gadsby in C, Branscombe in E flat, Bridge iu C, Hayne in E, with an organ recital (not without fuges) as a finale, they might, probably, as far as worship goes, be better at home. "Choirs should be largely disbanded. They are the weakness, not the strength, of the Church. Our churches generally, smaller ones especially, would worship infinitely better without them and their silly irrever- ence. Self-glorification plants itself only too success- fully in the choirister's seat. THE PARSON'S TRIAL.

..... "Choirs. it is well known, are the parson's trial, a remark which is particularly applicable to mixed choirs, with their three lively attendant devils, viz., the dress devil,tjae flirting devil, and the quarrelling Has not the Church of Rome, almost recently decreed 'No more mixed choirs ' ? And why be so enamoured of choirs, even of choirs which can sing? Why spend so freely on them when money is so urgently needed for other more pious uses ? " Waste in our churches is a common and much cherished sin ; the amount expended on music alone is prodigious. And so much of the music is so atrociously sung ! The gospel of simple worship is a necessary corollorary to the gospel of simple life. "GALLOP AND GABBLE."

-„-- " For prayer and praise our churches offer' gallop and gabble.' The Confession of Sin is apparently the merriest thing imaginable; it is rattled off on G at break- neck speed, as if it were the most joyful and laudable achievement to have erred and strayed from Thy ways like lost sheep,' and to have followed too much the devices and desires of our own hearts.' The sense of sin does not increase amongst us ; it is said to be pass- ing from us. Our churches are simply amazing ; they take one's breath away. The house of God has become the home of the world spirit. The worldly world has planted itself in the heart and centre of the Church, and has found welcome there. Pride, power, ambition, greed, partiality, dominate the Church still, though in a less obtrusive fashion than in the dark ages of her past. " As far as nominal Christianity is concerned, God is a dead God. He was the God of the past, He is not the God of the present, nor of the future."

div.p: NOVIIMBBIith 24 1906.
IT is evident that the THE PROBLENT action of the Government

OF THE RIND. with regard to the South African questions is being very much misunderstood. This, we suppose, was inevitable. In a much more real sense than Mr. 011AMBERIAIN'S war, it was impossible for the Government to do what was expected of it without incurring large liabilities, both of a financial and moral kind.TJndoubtedly the feeling of tile electors was that when a Liberal Govern ment,quite recently formed, wA reinstated by the General Election, there would be at once an end to Chinese serfdom, in South Africa; that, in fact, the Chinese would be at once deported, and that many of them would return to the prisons from which they came. Quite the reverse of this happened. The present Govern- ment permitted the use of the !sixteen thousand licenses for the importation of Chinamen, which had been issued by its predecessor just on the eve of its acceptance of office, and obviously with the I view of embarrassing its action. It was like honouring a fraudulent cheque. The public has a right to know what are the ri..-otives of Government policy in these matters and we believe that we are in a position to explain them. First of all, there is the financial question. It is of great magnitude, but we are convinced that the Government would not have considered it for a moment if it had stood by itself. We may as well, however, consider for a moment what it ,

means, for deportation of the Chinese coolies on the Rand is a liability devolving on the mine- owners, who have undertaken to repatriate their serfs at the end of their three years' con- tract. We do• not believe that they will be at all more willing to do this than they were willing to pay the £3,000000 for which they contracted with Mr. CHAMBERLAIN. rhey have defrauded the country before, and they will defraud it again. The cost of the repatriation of almost the whole, if riot quite the whole, of the Chinese on the Rand will devolve on the Imperial Government, hut the costs of repatriation would only represent a fraction of the Imperial liability. The breaking of the contracts would lead to illimitable actions at law against the Crown, and in each case damages would come out of the pockets of the people. This was a main reason, no doubt, for the acquiescence of the Government in the shameful transaction by which 16,000 new licenses were issued just before it took over the work of its predecessors. It is the guardian of the national purse, as well as of the national honour.

Nevertheless, the national purse would have suffered heavily but for other grave issues. The financial considerations would not by themselves have determined the action of the Government. What did determine its action was the desire to set up in the Transvaal a constitution which could not be attacked on merely party grounds. The great object was to secure the predominance of Liberal ideas, ideas that are not based on racial distinctions and that are not at the service of mere wealth. What would have happened if the Chinese had been ordered away from South Africa almost immediately after the present Government accepted office? The mines would have been shut down. There would have been a vast agitation both in South Africa and in this country. The ruin of the Rand would have been attributed to the action of the Liberal Ministry. The Government dew this. It perceived that its policy would be best served by letting the policy of the Randlords work itself out within the limit of time which is to be concluded by the establish- ment of the new Constitution. Can anyone say that the design has not admirably served its pur- pose ? The Randlords' system has overwhelmed itself with shame. Those South Africans who would have been now engaged in vituperating the Imperisl Government are now holding vast meet- ings to demand the repatriation of the Chinese and the Randlords have before them the spectacle of the catastrophe produced by their most immoral selfishness. A successful Liberal policy in South Africa has become possible just because the mperial Government has not been in too much of a hurry to enforce its views.

The Vicar of Burtonwood "RUNNING THE indulges in frequent out- CHURCHES." bursts of candour which cannot be other than dis- quieting to his brethren of the Church of England. In the current issue of his parish magazine, Mrr Mitchell denounces the churches and mostof thei- works with a vigour which would not have ill become an agnostic. The tendencies of the times • justify much that this outspoken clergyman says, and his criticisms should do more real good than actual harm. There is too much " running " of churches as we "run" the music or the concert hall and this is not the best way of reaching the masses "Pulpit romancing, choir concerts, stage perform- ances may attract and please the worldling, but do not tend to the reverent and devout worship'of Him Whose promised Presence never fails." We should like to say "hear, bear" with heartiness but we recognise that the Churches have a great difficulty in appealing to the people on purel; religious lines. Possibly the Church has beocnn worldly again, and while we agree that such worldiness must be challenged and dethroned, the reverend gentleman fails to suggest other practical means by which the Churches can get hold of the masses. Perhaps he is reserving suggestions for another article. It is easy ene to be a critic ! We should like to recom_ THE EDELSTEN mend the Warrington ACTION Corporation to Mr. S. . been a proper and ice examples of Gilbert, if the latter is at There has c complete farce with regard to the purchase of the aolrligdiensailrou comedy.sof findingrrhe Pin Mill in Knutsford-road from Mr. J. AL. Edelsten. First of all a bargain was struck between the then Mayor (Alderman Bolton) and Mr. Edelsten to purchase the property. The agree - ment was made but never received the Corporation seal or the consent of the Council. When the price became known the economists in the Council objected to the transaction being completed and carried their point. Then Mr. Edelsten threatened an action at law for completion of the agreement. The Council was very valorous, and after getting Counsel's opinion that they had a good defence determined to fight the case. They even indem- nified the Mayor, who was also cited to defend the action, and everyone thought that this £7,850 would not be paid except under compulsion. But all at (wee the Council has turned craven and last Friday night decided by a majority to settle the action and pay the costs in addition. Surely nothing could be more exasperating to the ratepayers or more laughable in the eyes of a disinterested onlooker ? The Corporation has behaved very much like the small boy who walks behind the big boy making fisticuff demonstra- tions, and then bolts without pause on the big boy turning round. We have seen nothing more ridiculous in municipal matters than this sudden climb-down on the part of the Council, and ' unfortunately it will probably cost the ratepayers dearly. No explanation was given at the Council meeting of the reason for such a reversal of policy. All discussion for and against had taken place beforehand at a General Purposes Committee meeting lasting two hours, and the Council was merely expected to confirm the decision already come to. Beyond a spirited pro- test by Council Pemberton, the proceedings were formal. This increases the unsatisfactory nature of a transaction which involves well over £BOOO and inquires further elucidation.

It is gratifying. to know INFIRMARY tat the Warrington MANAGEMENT. Infirmary enjoys a high reputation for economical management. So prominently does it stand out in this respect, in comparison with similar institu- tions, that a deputation from the Dewsbury Infirmary recently paid a visit of inspection to see if they could glean information which would be of advantage to them in the administration of their own funds. They were, we believe, very favourably impressed but after carefully going int( the matter they have decided that "for efficient am economical management, the balance of evidence is in favour of the Dewsbury institution," A resolm tion to this effect was confirmed at a meeting of thf Dewsbury Infirmary Board, and several speaker: made some interesting comparisons wbich we print in another column. Any little criticism which was offered was animated by a perfectly friendly spirit but it wilf perhaps be re-assuring to our readers if we explain several matters from the Warring- ton Board's standpoint. As Mr. Fitton stated, the Warrington Infirmary has two doctors 9 against Dewahury's one, but the necessity for t' larger medical staff must be obvious vv," we bear in mind the conditions with which , Warrington institution has to deal. Not onr is the accommodation of the Infirmary over-ta: with in-patients, but a great number of people treated in their own homes. In 1905 the numb, treated were : 1404 in-patients,39ol out-patients, and 3101 accidents. The Board have therefor-
