-felt it incumbent on them to engage one doctor to attend specially to outside work while the other remains at the Infirmary, and this of course means a higher sum for salaries. We are somewhat at a loss to account for Mr. Fitton's statement that "it was difficult ta probe to the lattom of things in Warrington's case, as no details were given in the reports, as was the case with Dewsbury's." The last annual report, which we'have before us, certainly presents a MASS of detail, every source of income and expenditure being carefully noted. If more minute particulars as to the disposal of drugs, food Jo., were to be given we are assured that more assistance would be required in the clerical department. We are not in a position to make exhaustive comparisons with Dewsbury, as no returns from that institution have been sent to Burdett's " Hospitals and Charities "—the recognized year book—for several years and the *Warrington Secretary has not yet been favoured with a copy of the annnal report. It is surprising to find one speaker at the Dewsbury Board meeting asserting that " at Warrington they had not behind them such a noble army of workingmen as Dewsbury had." The Warring- ton Workingmen's Committee has a splendid record of devoted work, and their enthusiasm on behalf of the Institution was never greater. In 1901 the amount raised oy the Committee was £742 17s. 51. whereas last year it had grown to £94.5. It is confidently hoped that this year £l,OOO will be handed over. Warringtonians have every reason to feel satisfied that their Infirmary is being most economically worked, and we would take this opportunity of again urging the ,claims of the extension scheme—a biz undertaking which has been forced upon the Board by the ever- increasing pressure on the accommodation. The response has already been generous, but over £5,000 is still required bafora the necessary £15,000 is raised.

-- Our appeal to the Powers SHALL TEM three years ago on the CoNso HORROgs question of the Congo Cogrnsum ? horrors was apparently pro- ductive of no good result ; since then, the report of the Commission of Inquiry has been issued, and, as Sir Edward Grey told the influential deputation which waited upon him, it • is not unlikely that another appeal would have a different result to-day. England may assure the Powers that new she desires to see this matter through. France has become our friend, and • France holds a right of pre-emption, and is by treaty next heir after Belgium to the lands of the Congo Free State. To-day these exist only for the State to make, by every means it can enforce, profit out of rubber. The Belgian Parliament has never intervened. The shares have been split into fractions and widely distributed ; and there is a theory, which is legally assisted, that the Congo is a private estate of Xing Leopold. Rubber is not obtained by trade; it is exacted as tribute. It requires the labour of every adult male for eleven or twelve days " in very fortnight. The Italian Government have made their observations on the spot, and forbiddden any more officers of their Army to enter the service of the Congo Free State. If the Bllgian Legislature declines to annex, it is for the Powers in concert to say that sornethieg shall be done. The situation is serious. Tales, harrow:log enough, have been told of the barbarities perpetrated on rubber slaves, and such records become the more shocking when they are contrasted with the professions on which the Free State was founded. We do not wish to lecture Belgium ; but we desire that some action shall be taken. If the gravity and the humanity of the case do not move her. our duty will become clear to sound the other Powers as to further inquiry and common action.

The claim is made by a TEST/N Criatsrux community at Bielefield. in Socumsai. I'Vestphalia, that it is follow- ing the Golden Rule rather than the rule of gold. Strange to relate, the system seems to be workable. People who are failures in life are got into discipline there. It is ' ' : traced to the old.fashioned trust in the Bible, and 1 pit'. toi the example of Psstor ,von Bodelschwingh ard ' ferkt from R 6 wife, both raised in aristocratic circles' who 1 Berlin to undertake this work. First 7 all there is a home called Ebenezer for Eoilep. 1 tics, and when anyone thinks of the terrible buffat_ iog these people get when they are poor and have to fight their ocvn battle in the world the value of such an asylum, where work can be honestly and quietly done, wilt be appreciated. Another Home is for training nurses, and a third for training deacons, and these install- 1 tions give a good influence to some whizli are designed for setting broken wills. There is one colony for wealthy voluntary patients who have made shipwreck of life through drink or fast living or both, and with physical comforts and industrial labour are building themselves up again. Still another home is for those who can find no opening elsewhere because they have been COD- victod of theft or embezzlement or dishonesty of some kind. The crowning triumph perhaps is that close on a thousand of the lodgers at the "Tramps Rouse" have, after being there a while, got regular employment. This training of,degenerates') of weaklings, and of persons bordering on moral imbecility is a terrible test of patience. But the highest type of Christian leader can do it. Corn pared with it,tickling, the ears of a large congrega- tion by preaching is child's play.

Wesley Guild Lecture. The members of the Bewsey-road Wesley Guild sPent a very enjoyable evening on Monday when Mr. Kenneth Bishop, who is a skilful and enthusiastic photographer, exhibited a fine collection of lantern slides illustrating scenery in North Wales. The slides were Mr. 'Bishop's own work, and were of a highly artistic character. As a contrast a number of scenes of juvenile life in Warrington streets were thrown on the screen. The pictures were all interestingly erplained, and the lecture vras greatly appreciated.

The offer of 10s. in the S, by Mr. J. Havelock- Wilson, ALP., has been accepted by the majority of his creditors. *
We may as well make up our minds to tackle the overdue task of destroying the House •of Lords. It has to be done sooner or later, and sooner the better. —" Star."

If shopkeepers and others only bore in mind the motto of a London grocer, there would be less work for the Bankruptcy Court. The motto of the trades- man referred to was "Trust in the Lord ; everyone else cash." . .

* * * The juvenile population of Warrington, and possibly many "01(1 boys" too, will feel a pang of regret at the disappearance of that one-time popular place of amusement, the Circus in Queen-street. This week workmen have been busily engaged in pulling down the building,and no longer will the quips and cranks of the clown and thrilling exploits in the arena afford delight on winter evenings. * * * The Rev. J. F. Matthews is nothing if not original. After recent experiences at a number of gatherings be has come to the conclusion that formal votes of thanks are "unmitigated nuisances," and at the annual sale of work in connection with Latchford Baptist Church on Thursday they were dispensed with. Many people will agree with Mr. Matthews, for votes of thanks are often such obvious matters of form as to be scarcely complimentary.

4 During the past year a remarkable attendance record has been established by the children of Foulden School in Norfolk. The average attendance comes out at 99.5 per cent., and 90 per cent, of the children are entitled to medals for being present every time the school was open. Thirteen of the scholars are also to be awarded medals for tnree year's perfect attendance. Only one infant lost an attend- ance during the year.

* There was an amusing little incident at the meeting of the Education Committee on Monday evening. By a slip of the tongue Councillor Ellison, instead of moving the confirmation of the minutes of the School Attendance Committee, of which he is chairman, pro- posed the confirmation of the committee itself. The error had passed unnoticed until Mr. A. J. Jolley casually inquired " when the ceremony would take place "and hinted that he would like to be present. *s*

Some funny things occasionally happen at meet- ings of local representative bodies but it is a long time since we heard of anything to equal an incident which occurred at Morley (nVar Dewsbury) Counci!. The discussion had to do with the origin of a fire which had occurred in the town ; and one enlightened individual had suggested " spontaneous combustion " as the probable cause. "Sir," said another aum- cillor, " there was not an ounce of it about the place!"

* * * Yesterday's Local Government Board inquiry at the Town Hall was quite a novelty in its way. Not a single opponent or questioner pet in art appear ance and the proceedings lasted barely half an hour. There is a consensus of opinion as to the necessity of street paving being carried out as early as possible, especially in the nPighbonthood of Such a building as the Beamont School which will be in use early next year.

* * * By the d.eath of Councillor Brough a great many people in Warrington will miss a worthy man and a kindly friend. Mr.Brough was one of those men who endeavoured to go through the world smiling. It is sad to reflect that his cheeriness was sorely tried by the painful nature of the malady which ultimately brought about his death—in fact his end could only be looked upon as a happy release. 'Tis often the best among men who are the most severely tried. * * * After the trouble in Stockton Heath over tree- planting the " Heathen" have decided to expend their surpluk energy in another direction. Last week it was decided to form a Stockton Heath District Nursing Association, to be run on similar lines to the sister organization in Warrington, and if this new departure is welcomed with an amount of enthusiasm equal to that displayed over tree-planting, its success is assured. We sincerely hope this will prove the case as there is undoubted need for such a body in the district.

* * We understand that the Sub-Committee appointed to report on those trees in Stockton Heath which are considered either dangerous or a nuisance has pro- nounced judgment on at least 30 trees which will have to be removed. They are principally in the White- field-road district. The tree-planting anniversary is also to be celebrated to-day, and several ladies will plant further trees in Grappenhall-road, where there is ample room. Perhaps some economy could be effected by utilising the condemned trees from Whitefiald-road. ' We offer the suggestion for what it is worth—which is perhaps not much at this late hour. * During last summer 1,10(5 boys from the elementary schools attended the baths regularly and 99 learnt to swim, while 47 were already able to do so. Arrange- ments are to be made in the future for proper instruction, but even then the lack of accommodation must be a sad problem. All the boys cannot get into one plunge bath, and the girls have no opportunities at all. It seems to us that branch swimnaing baths would be as valuable to the community as branch libraries until the day dawns when each school has its own plunge bath and a course of compulsory education in swimming. The question is in our view, of much greater import than teaching the youngsters the use of the rifle, but it does not receive one hundredth of the attention. _

The tram was full—what the conductor, confiding to the trolley-boy, called " fairly tight." There were not, however, as yet any strap-hangers. The passengers were fairly comfortable, and with the natural selfishness of tram passengers they were pray- ing that no one else 'would come in. One side of the car was hopelessly full, and on that side people felt safe from further squashing. On the other side there was ope less than the regular number, but things were no better, because it was a row of singularly sub- stantial people. A lady, expansive and anxious, boarded the car. The conductor's face became a little more drawn than before. " Revrm on this side," he bawled, looking down the tout row. "Oh, surely not," said a despairing old gentleman on that side. The conductor turned a tragic face upon hum. "I canna help their boolk," he said—" Manchester Guardian."

,e • ~t S The Lords hare not shown very great capacity .to understand the intricacies of the Education Bill, though they have been in no doubt as to what they wanted. On Monday, Lord Crewe tested their intelli- gence in an amusing fashion. Some question of rating having arisen, the Lord President of the Council ex- plained it by reference to a section in the Act of 1902, which provides that the grant for a certain purpose from the Exchequer should be calculated on the scale of "three halfpence for every twopence by which the I product of a penny rate falls below ten shillinge for every child in average attendance." The Lords who are not nimble-witted staggered under this blow, and Lord Londonderry passed his hand across his fore- head as who should say." Am I going mad " ? amiably at the effect he had produced, Lord Crewe genially offered a prize to any peer whc could work out the sum offhand. No 'lordly hand was raised to indicate that its owner had the answer ready, and the prize remains unwon.

Proposed Milk Combine. The milk producers in the mid-Cheshire district are determined to protect their interests as against those of the seller, who has, it is urged, been too long dictator to the farmer in regard to the price for milk-. , A price list association has been formed, and at a largely-attended meeting it has been decided to appeal for the co-operation of all dairy farmers in Cheshire, ! Lancashire, Staffordshire, Derbyshire, and Shropshire, ! and to invite them to send two representatives each to. a conference to be held in mid-Cheshire, so that uniform action may be taken. WooD CHIMNEY PIECES, Fire Grates and Tiles. unrivalled selection, inspection invited.—J. S, GARLAND, Builders' Ironmonger, 51 to 55, Bridge at., Warrington.—Advt. " Y " Branch B.W.T.A. An open meeting of the above society was held at , the Winmarleigh Cafe on Wednesday evening. Mrs.! Dunn (W. J.) was in the chair, and after a short address introduced Rev.C.Harvey Cook,as the speaker of the evening, who in the course of his remarks expressed the opinion that societies nowadays —and people in general—were inclined to be too serious. They didn't laugh enough. A speech was often lacking in point through being short of humour and people missed their full share in the pleasure and experiences , of life for the same reason. He also didn't feel quite ! sure whether a society formed only of one sex, like I the "Y's ", would ever give the large benefit a mixed! one might. The tendency seemed to be to divide and sub- divide societies to a very great extent, and he, person- ally didn't see why they shouldn't all work more as one , family. Also people were too parochial in their ideas! and emotions:They didn't feel sufficiently one with the universe—didn't live their lives fully. He then went ! on to point out that the success of a society rested on the lives the individual members of that society led. Unit is they themselves, were giving their very best Meryday life, they couldn't expect their public life to bear much fruit. Among many helpful ideas ! be suggested that in the summer, the members might go into the poorer quarters of the town and give out- door concerts, so giving pleasure and brightening the lives of many in need of recreation. The temperance cause was better helped by actions of this description, than by long lectures and lurid descriptions of the evils of drink. They shouldn't talk about drunken- ness, but about abstinence; and their object should be to give pleasure to their less fortunate sisters. The meeting closed with the usual vote of thanks to the speaker and chairmasn. The names were also included of MisS Cox for two delightful songs and Miss liltndrick for an excellent recitation. " HERALD " KITCHEN RANG ES and " Peveril " , Fire Grates are hard to beat.—Sole agent, J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55, Bridge st., Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: " OLIVER AND CO."
div.p: " OLIVER AND CO."
A Warrington Bankrupt at the Assizes.

Oliver Summers, a boot dealer who formerly traded at Warrington as Oliver and Co., was charged under several indictments,before Mr. Justice Sutton and a jury, in the Crown Court at Manchester Assizes on Thursday. It was stated that on December 4th last he was adjudged a bankrupt at the Manchester Bankruptcy Court, and it was alleged that he did not reveal to the Official Receiver all his real and persoaal property, that he failed to deliver to the Official Receiver £2OO realised on the sale of 553 pairs of boots and shoes,that be made a material omission in his statement of affairs, and that he attempted to destroy documents relating to the sale of his boots.
Mr. Byrne and Mr. Henriques appeared for the prose- cuticn, and Mr. Gibbons aapeared for the defence. . .

Mr. Byrne stated that Slimmers had two shops iu War- rington up to August, 1905, and after that date carried on business at one shop in Bridge-street. Early in November he was in a state of insolvency, and execu- tions were levied. The sheriff's officer took possession of the stock at the shop for a debt of £lOl. The stock was 1,031 pairs of boots and shoes, and the value was from £450 to £5OO. The accused, after consultation with his solicitor, called in Mr. Hickman, a local auctioneer, who bought the stock for £BO. For two or three days an auction was held, and £9O was realised. The prisoner made up the remainder of the money required by the sheriff's officer, who left. 533 pairs of boots valued at £2OO were then handed back to Summers Before the end of December he had sold 469 pairs for £l6O. On the 4th December, on his preliminary examina- tion in bankruptcy, he declared that on the 25th of November he had sold his stock in trade for £lOl to Mr. Hickman, who had since sold by auction all the stock on the premises. In his statement of affairs he said his' unsecured liabilities amounted to £1,272 and his assets to £l6l, "cash in hand of the sheriff." That meant that ths assets were nil, and no allusion was made to the stock of boots or the proceeds of the stock left in his hands. In February the Official Receiver granted a warrant for the searching of the house of the prisoner's mother-in- law, who was a boot and shoe dealer at Earlestown. When the Assistant Official Receiver and the bailiff entered the house the prisoner pulled out a brindle of papers, one of which he attempted to destroy by tearing it into pieces. The bailiff recovered the pieces, which showed that the prisoner had sold 469 pairs of boots and had received for them £l6ll. The officers also found a cash register and a roll of paper showing the takings at the shop for three months up to the time of bank- ruptcy. Neither of these things was accounted for at the examination. It was also found that book debts for £42 had not been mentioned. The evidence of several witnesses for the prosecu- tion occupied the Court for five hours. Representatives of the Official Receiver and Messrs. Hickman, senior and junior, auctioneers, of Warrington, were called by Mr. Byrne to bear out his opening statement. Following Mr. F. Hickman's evidence as to the circumstances attending the purchase of the prisoner's stock, Mr. Johnston,assistant official receiver, said the first he knew of the transfer of the surplus stock from Hickman to the prisoner was through a letter written by Hickman's solicitor in February. Witness, with an inspector and a bailiff, made a search at the prisoner's shop at Earlestown. They found the prisoner there, and on proceeding to search the premises they came across some stock, which the prisoner explained had been consigned to him for sale by a Wigan man. Summers took from his pocket a bundle of papers to show they had been consigned to him, but when asked for them he refused to give them up, and tore one paper in two. The bailiff was called and told to take the papers from him. The prisoner then handed the papers to him. Reference was also made to the discovery of the cash register which the prisoner said he sold to a brother. When asked what he did with the money he received for the boots sold, prisoner said he paid it all awayin expenses. To ascertain the truth of that state- ment, said Mr. Byrne, they had to analyse the cash account, which presented all the money he had paid away. The evidence of Mr. Johnston had not concluded when the court adjourned. YESTERDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.
Mr. Ellis Johnson, assistant official receiver, was cross-examined by Mr. Gibbons upon the evidencehe gave on Thursday. Other witnesses gave evidence on behalf of the prose- cution.

The defendant then gave his own account of the transaction with Mr. Hickman, the auctioneer. He said he made an out-and-out sale of his stock to Mr. Hickman for £BO, and there was no arrangement that when that £BO had been realised he was to have the remainder of the stock returned to him. He could not say how many !Snots remained on the premises, and handed over the key to him. He had drawn about .£7O since for the sale of boots, and he gave an account of hriw this money had been spent. He denied that he had concealed any of his property from the Official Receiver, or that he had put any money into his own pocket unknownl.to the Official Receiver. His explanation of destroyinfirthe document spoken to by the prosecution was that he thought it was a piece 1 of waste paper. Cross-examined : He admitted that he was insolvent when he consulted Hickman. but he would not have been pushed by the cash creditors. What he did was for the benefit of his creditors. Mr. Gibbons, in his address to the jury, argued that the defendant had not defrauded his creditors. The jury found Summers guilty. Sentence was post- poned until to-day.

div.head: SCIENCE & SUPERSTITION. ' RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: SCIENCE & SUPERSTITION. ' RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

QUESTION IN PARLIAMENT. , Mr. Seddon is to ask the Home secretary, in the House of Commons on Tuesday, whether he will inquire into the treatment of two female members of the Salvation Army by the Widnes police, who forced 'them to wash in the presence of three police officers notwithstanding a protest made by the women. ANTT-VACCINATIONISTS AT RUNCORN. Edward Williams, 5, Victoria-road, Runcorn, applied to Messrs. James Pritchard and D. Bisbrown at the Runcorn Sessions on Monday, for a certificate exempt- ing him from having his child vaccinated. He stated the usual legal formular. The Chairman asked him if he bad any special reason. He replied that he did not think the child was strong enough to stand the risk of vaccination. Harry Holt, 10, Balfour-street, and John Edgar Johnson, 5, Lightburn-straet, made similar applications. The certificates were granted. A RUNCORN BOY HERO. The usual course of study at the Runcorn Institute Secondary School and Pupil Teachers' Centre was the other afternoon slightly and in a most unusual way varied. It will be remembered that in June last a former scholar of the school sacrificed his life in a futile attempt to rescue a friend from drowning in the rivar Weaver. W. C. Williams, the boy referred to had, as the holder of a Cheshire County Council scholar- ship, attended the school for seven terms, during which period he had become a univeral favourite with all connected with the "Teo." His unvarying attention to his studies and respectful manner towards his instruc- tors was conspicuous and when he succeeded in obtaining work he left the school much to the regret of his teachers and fellow-scholars. Although Williams was no longer a day scholar when the fatality occurred, it was decided that the school should be represented at the funeral, and a wreath was subscribed for. After , the purchase of a wreath a substantial sum remained in ' hand, and a suggestion was made that a permanent token of respect should be placed in the school. This took the form of a massive brass memorial tablet, which has been placed in the main corridor, in a most promin- ent position. The tablet bears the following inscription: —" In memory of W. C. Williams, who lost his life 9th June, 1906, in trying to rescue a friend from drowning. This tablet is placed here here by his teachers and fellow-scholars." WIDNES BOY SENT TO A REFORMATORY. At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, before Alderman Wareing (in the chair) and Alderman S. Quinn, John Mitchell (14), a diminutive boy, who resides with his widowed mother at 66, Midwood-street, was charged with breaking into the lock-up shop, 36, Widnes-road, with felonious intent.—Superintendent Strickland said that owing to serious robberies which had occurred at Mr. Alfred Edwards' " Minerva" Printing Works, a constable was put to watch. A short time ago a window in the works was broken sufficiently to admit a.boy. On Saturday night some cardboard was put against it. P.C. Jones was concealed inside, and at 10.15 p.m. he saw the prisoner scale a wall behind the shop. He searched seine drawers but did not beet anything. Jones arrested him, and charged him with the offence, and he replied "You are right." There was another charge against the prisoner of breaking into the same shop and stealing 10s. Id. a short time before.He pleaded guilty to that also. —Alfred Edwards printer and stationer, coi:oborated. Witness had missed the sum of 10s. 6d. from the shop a short time ago.—The boy pleaded guilty, and his mother elected for him to be summarily dealt with.—Superin- tendent Strickland said the prisoner had received three strokes of the birch rod for stealing a carriage lamp in January, 1901.—1 n reply to the Chairman, the lad's mother said he was beyond her control. She was a widow, with seven children, and earned her living by washing.—Alderman Wareing said the prisoner was an extremely bad boy, and unless he was taken in hand at once he would live a career of crime. He would have to go to a reformatory school until he was 19 years of age. MORE SALVATIONISTS FINED AT WIDNES. . MAGISTRATES ADVICE TO THE ARMY. At Widnes Police Court on Thursday, before Alderman Quinn and Alderman Waring, Messrs. C. E. Turnbleton and Albert Mahe, Sarah Morris, Mary Houghton, Eva M'Leod and Caroline Ratcliffe, six Salvationists, were charged with obstructing the free passage of Victoria- square on October 27th.—Sergeant Blakeloy stated that at 7.15 on the evening in question he saw about thirty people taking part in the Salvation Army service at the big lamp, and at 7.35 the crowd hed increesed to the dimensions of seventy. Witnes thought pedestrians were obstructed on their way. to the Widnes Market. He requested the Salvationists to move away, and on their refusing to do so he took their names. Ma- Frost, for the defence, said there was not one case of substantial obstruction of the highway, as alleged by the police. In this case a police officer stated that certain pedestrians had to go a roundabout way, and there were no objections by them that any obstruction has been caused. The Bench had said on a previous occasion that they felt that an offence had been com- mitted, and imposed a fine, but upon that judgment men and women had been taken to prison. The Salvation Army had a conscientious conviction that they had a right to stand in the place so long as they did not infringe the rights of the citizens.— Mr. Frost called no evidence, and a fine of Is. and costs was imposed in each case, the Caairman (Alder- man Waring) stating that they would state a case.— Another batch of eight salvationists named W.A. 1\ lame, Prescot ; J. Steele, Norwich ; Gertrude Vicary, Mold; Albert Grainger, Liverpool; Earnest Blackman,Prescot ; ldary A. Wal,h, Rhos; Griffiths Rob arts, Widnes ; and William Hill, Widnes, were also similarly charged for an offence on the 3rd of November.—Police evidence of obstruction Was given by Sergeant Davidson and Sergeant Waters.—The Chairman, Major Waring, raid that in these cases the fines would be 10s.and costs each or fourteen days, and he asked the members of the Salvation Army to seriously consider the offer made to them by the Council with respect to the new sites which had been offered them. and which were equally as , good and as public us that of the big lamp.

div.head: [By W. Clirimes.]
div.p: [By W. Clirimes.]

- - The return of Halley's Comet, which is supposed to be identical with the Star of Bethlehem, may at any moment become a aubject of world-wide and general interest. So long since as 1894 some observatories began to make preparations for tracing it line of approach. It was then said to be within the orbit of Neptune. The eyes of science saw it coming 12 years ago, and though it may be still far away it is coming earthwards with great velocity. The appearances of this large and brilliant comet have been recorded with more or less detail and regularity from the earliest times, but it was not until after its visit in 1682 that any plausible theory was propounded as to its movements. Sir Isaac• Newton came to the con- clusion that this celestial wanderer is a periodical visitor to the neighbourhood of our sun, and that it travels in a long eliptical orbit. When nearest it is about .56,000,000 miles from the sun, and a consider- able distance inside the earth's orbit. When farthest away it is about 3,370,000,000 miles from the sun, and far beyond the limits of the planetary system at present known. Its last visit was in 1835, and it will be seen from subsequent dates that the intervals vary frona 70 to 80 years, so that probably it has been on its return journey earthward and sunward about 35 years. Astronomers are now busy calculating the exact date of its arrival. As the variation has been from five to 10 years, there is perhaps as much guess- ing as calculating. One astronomer tries to explain this great variation by suggesting that it may be caused by the perturbing influences affecting the ; comet's motion. Perhaps so. But that seems ! to me rather a perturbing suggestion. No well ! regulated comet would go wandering about aimlessly for years. Perhaps the variation is more i apparent than real. In several cases I auspect either the records or the comets have got a little mixed. I Let us tern from the scientific to the superstitious ! side, or shall we say to the historical coincidencies. ! These are at least interesting and in some cases ! remarkable. I have alluded to the "Star of Bethlehem "which was probably the celestial wanderer now known as Halley's Comet for the following reasons: It seems certain that Halley's Comet appeared a,short time (probably four years) before ; the Birth of Christ. That it travelled southwards corresponding with the journeying of the wise men, after seeing Herod, from Jerusalem to Bethlehem and the assumption that it would have a meridian culmination low down, is consistent with the Bible story about the wise men rejoicing when they saw the star again. Had it been travelling in another direc- tion it would probably have been visible early in the evening, and they would have had no anxiety about its re-appearance. This theory is supported by the fact that in 1835 when the observations were accurate and reliable Halley's Comet took a similar course. We are told that this comet appeared again, 70 years after the Nativity. Again when Antony the First began his reign. It :passed across the sky when the Goths were threatening Rome and again in the time of Diocletian: It was watched with awe and wonder by the hordes of invading Huns. It caused consternation and dismay amongst the hosts of Kino. Attila when he was defeated at Chalons in 451. The magnificent spectacle of this comet in the heavens is said to have been the inspiration of Mahornet. lor several centuries the records and references appear to be uncertain and it would seem that nothing either celestial or terrestrial could illumine the dark ages. We pass to the year 1066 when we are told that Halley's comet, during the Battle of Hastings, shone with exceeding brilliance, and shed as it were, a glow of splendour over the Norman Conquest. If this is only coincidence it is almost as wonderful as that which happened over a thousand years before at Bethlehem. Let us pause fcir a moment to consider what would have been the result had William of Normandy been defeated on the field of Senlac and driven from the shores of Britain. Is it not in the highest degree probable that the march of civilization would have been retarded for centuries ? Might not the history of the world have been altogether different? As it was, the fusion of two widely different races has had the most momentous consequences. On the one hand was the sturdy, stubborn all enduring Saxon with his I love of homely and material comforts. On the other' was Norman chivalry, martial ardour, poetic fervour and genius tor organization. These with the advan- tage of an insular'position, were the best possible materials for the formation of a conquering race as events have proved. Proceeding with the references to Halley's comet,we find that its awe inspiring appearance was coin- raemorated by the hand of Queen Matilda in the Bayeux Tapestry. In 1223 it was thought to be a ! portent of the death of Phillip Augustus. In 1301 it caused world-wide astonishment. In 1456, the year of the Battle of Belgrade it terrified both Christians and Turks and was anathematised by the Pope. In this year its tail was about 40 degrees long. It is supposed that the Chinese have the most complete , records about this comet, but they are closely and ! jealously guarded, as in some mysterious way the dynasty and destiny of China are said to be indicated. Finally it is thought quite possible that sooner or later this comet may fall into the sun, if it does not get steadier in its ways and mode of travelling. Whether in such a case anything serious might happen is not quite clear. The chance I sup- pose if only one in many millions. Let us hope that if this occurs at some distant period, the inhabitants, will be rather better prepared that we are at present. I mean better prepared as regards a wider knowledge of those truths which bring philosophic calm and resignation. Those who like the late W. H. Myers have " a deep scientific conviction that their is a deathless soul in man " need not fear any catastrophe which is possible or conceivable in a material sense. There is no scientific evidence in support of annihilation or of finality. Those who admit the indestructibility of matter and yet doubt the continuity of life, or the persistence and immortal nature of that which shapes and animates matter, are to say the least deficient in reasoning power. For my part Ido not believe that since the dawn of creation a single being has perished or ceased to exist.

div.head: HARDY ANNUAL.
div.p: A HARDY ANNUAL.
Latchford Baptist Sale of Work.

For a number of years it has been found necessary at Latchford Baptist Church to hold an annual sale of work to suppliment the income of the church, which whilst showing a yearly increase isnot sufficient to meet the expenses incurred. This year's venture was held on Thursday in the schoolroom, Wash lane and was again a success, £42 being realized as against £39 last year. The Rev. J. F. Matthews explained that month by month last year the income of the church exceeded that of the previous year, and returns this year showed a similarly gratifying result—a result attained without any badgering or cadging or even formal solicitations from the pulpit. Last year the offerings realized £1.20 whilst the total income of the church was £250 and at the close of the year they had a balance in hand of £3O. He was hoping that before long they would be able to maintain the church without having to hold an annual sale. (Applause). The Rev. J. Yonge who presided, said that when Mr. Matthews spoke of a balance in hand he made his mouth water. At Wycliffe Cnurch they generally had a balance on the wrong side and had to do something to get rid of it. He hoped that having got a balance in hand they would maintain it. (Applause). Mrs. C. E. Parker said she was sorry to hear Mr. Matthews say that in time there would be no need for the sale. To have something to work for gave them a stimulous and, besides, the weekly gatherings of the workers brought people together and enabled many who could not afford to give money to give time and labour to the Church. Mr. Parker and herself were intensely interested in every kind of Free Church, in fact their Free Churchism was much stronger than any other particular ism, and they were very glad to identify themselves with every Free Church which needed help. She had pleasure in declaring the sale open and in wishing it every Success. (Applause.) The stalls which bore a large assortment of useful and ornamental articles, and which afforded ample evidence of the self denying labours of the congregation were in charge of the following ladies : Refreshment stall : Mrs. Fairhurst and friends, plain stall: Mrs. Adams and friends; fancy stall : Mrs.gatthews and friends ; dairy stall, Mesdames Williams. Wilkinson and friends; young men's stall, Mr. J. R. Conway and friends ; penny stall: Mrs. Ackerley and friends ; stationery stall : Miss C. Pearson and friends. During the proceedings humorous competitions wore held whilst Mr. Alfred Grounds afforded pleasure with his humorous items.

div.head: EVAN ROBERTS "VEGETATING."
div.p: EVAN ROBERTS "VEGETATING."

- Evan Roberts, the Welsh revivalist, is staying at Leicester with his friends, Mr. and Mrs. Penn Lewis. He is still unfit for work, or even study. Under medical orders he is vegetating74iving i.n.the.fresh air, taking gentle exercise, and living on a rigid diet.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.

WEAK MILK AT BURTONWOOD. At the Warrington County Sessions on Wednesday, John Orford, milkdealer, Broad-lane, Burtonwood, was summoned for selling adulterated mik which contained 12 per cent. of water. For the defence it was contended that the milk was sold to the inspector as it was received from the farmer.—The defendant had nothing whatever to do with the business. The magistrates imposed a fine of 40s. and costs. ACCIDENT AT THE VIADUCT WORKS. On Saturday morning an enployee at the Es,rlestown Viaduct works, named William Riche, of Cross-lane,was following hts employment when a plate fail on his foot which was badly crushed, the small toe being completely severed. He was immediately taken some and medically attended.

div.head: PUPPY SHOW.
div.p: PUPPY SHOW.

The members of the local dog society held a most successful puppy show at the Ram's Head Hotel, Earles- town, last week. The principal winners were :—White haired terrier, Mr. Downham ; English terrier, Mr. F. Birkhead ; English bull,Mr. J. Davenport ; Irish terrier, Mr. J. Barrows ; fox terrier, Mr. G. Sturgess. Mr. B. Birkhead's spaniel was awarded a consolation piize. Mr. J. Goodfan was the judge. The exhibits had bean staged by Mr. W. Beatty. CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH. The Rev. J. Davidson having completed his first year as pastor of Newton Congregational Church, services to mark the " pastor's anniversary "were held last Svaday Dr. Gaul's cantata "Ruth," was given in the afternoon by an enlarged choir,with Misses tloward,Grace Bothell and Elsie Barr, and Mr. J. White, as soloists. There were large congregations at each service. RETIREMENT OF A WELL-KNOWN NEWTONIAN. The retirement of Mr. J. Owen on a well-deserved I pension, after 44 years' service at the Newton-le-Willows Reformatory as master shoemaker, took place last week and his leaving the district for Heswall, Cheshire, occasioned much regret among his many friends at Newton aud Earlestown. Prior to his departure the officers of the school presented him with a gold mounted umbrella' and the master and matron made him the recipient of a brass standard lamp. He was accompanied , to the railway station by the school band under the ' conductorship of Superintendent J. Digweed, and as the train left the boys sang" Auld lang syne." MR. BOTTOMLEY AND RELIGIOUS TRAINING. On Sunday afternoon Mr. J. EL Bottonaley, the Con- ' servative agent for the Newton Division, delivered an address at 6 Golborne to an audience of men. He strongly urged theta to keep up their connection NNith their church and school, and the older men to send their children to such schools as would ensure their receiving a religious education. They must remember that the boys of to-day would be the parents of to-morrow, and the public guardians of the day after. He also impressed on those present the necessity of all men writing their names by kindness, love, charity, honesty. decision courage, and good example on the hearts of hose they came in contact with.

div.head: ST HELENS. . --- CIVIC FUNCTION.
div.p: ST HELENS. . --- CIVIC FUNCTION.

. -- The Mayoress of St. Helens (Mrs. Bishop) held the first of her annual "at homes" at the Town Hall on Tuesday, when the mayoral apartments were beautifully decorated. The Carmen Sylva Orchestra rendered, selections of music, and there was a large attendance of residents. FAMILY AFFRAY. PUNISHMENT FOR STABBING WIFE. Joseph Greenhalgh, labourer, of 70, Silkstone-street, was charged at St. Helens, on Monday with wounding his wife by stabbing her.—Mrs. Greenhalgh said that on Saturday, the 3rd inst., her husband came home druelf. A quarrel arose between Mrs. Greenhalgh and her sister. Greenhalgh told them to stop. The wife struck him on the head with a cup, and ran outside. He followed, and, after a struggle on the ground, Mrs. Greenhalgh was picked up, and found to be bleeding seriously from two wounds—one in the lower part of the breast and one near the top of the thigh. When Chief-inspector Goodall came on the scene the house was full of women, screaming and urging on two men who were fighting, stripped to the waist.—The Chief Constable agreed to reduce the charge to aggravated

assault.—Greenhalgh nleaded guilty to this, but said that he was upset and irritated by the quarrelling. He struck her, but did not remember having a knife in his hand. He was sorry for the occurrence.—The Chair- man said Greenhalgh would have been heavily punished at the assizes, but they would send him to gaol for five months. ST. HELENS LABOURER'S DEATH. Mr. Brighouse, county coroner,in openiug the inquest at St.Helens on Wednesday on William Tynan, aged 45, Bold-street,vvho was found dead in a saltcake waggon at ' Messrs Pikington's works on Tuesday, said that the case appeared a simple one. He had, however, found so often that if he dispensed with an inquest in a case where a man died at any works all sorts of disputes ,arose if the case was not fully investigated. He had, therefore, held an inquest, and a post-mortem had been made.—Mrs. M'Crory, deceased's niece, with whom h e lived, said that up to dinner-time on Monday Tynan was well. He was a single man, and lived with her. Deceased had suffered from rupture for about ten years. —John M'Cabe, of 45, Waterloo-street, said that on Monday afternoon abopt four o'clock, Maria Murphy called his attention to the saltcake waggon which deceased was discharging. He found Tynan at the bottom of the waggon moaning.—Police-constable Forster said he was called to the place, and removed the man to the surgery, but he thought he was dead when he got to him.—Dr. Unsworth gave details of the post-mortem. and said he found the cavity of the heart completely filled with blood,which had come from a rup- ture of the aorta close by. The aorta as dilated,and the walls considerably thinned. The wall of the aorta had burst, and the man would die very suddenly. It would only be a matter of seconds. The cause of death was aneurism of the aorta, intra-pericardial rupture and syncope.—The jury returned a verdict accordingly.

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

Coming Events. The grand Liberal Soiree will be held at the Lion Hotel on December oth. It is hoped that all tickets will be purchased by December Ist in order that the whist drive may be properly arranged. The annual meeting in connection with the War- rington District Nursing Association will be held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, on Tuesday. Mr. F. Monks will preside. The annual tea in connection with the Warrington Women's Liberal Association will be held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, on Monday. In the evening an address on Free Trade will be delivered by Miss K. Ashworth Briggs. Tea will be on the tables at 7.0 p.m. The Mayor and Mayoress (Alderman and Mrs. Smethurst) will hold an " At Home " at the Town Hall on December 6th, from 3 to 5.30 p.m. A grand concert will be held in the Parr Hall on Monday evening in aid of the funds of the Warrington District Nursing Association. An excellent pro- gramme has been arranged and the following artistes will appear : Miss Evangeline Florence, soprano; Miss Esther Yunson, contralto ; Mr. John Bardsley, tenor : Mr. Emlyn, Davies, baritone ; Miss A. Back- sheen Wood, violinit ; Mr. Lyndon Wyatt and Hiss Carrie Lumbers. Particulars as to prices, &c., will be found en page'. A charity concert in aid of the widow and family of the late Mr. J. Fagan, of Orford lane, will be held in Parr Hall on Monday, December 3rd. The circum- stances are extraordinarily sad. Mr. Fagan has only been dead about six months, and since then, a son and two daughters have also succumbed. At the present time, the one son left at home of a working age is suffering from that dread disease, consumption, and is unable to follow his employment. To add to this two younger children are also invalids, suffering from the same disease. Further particulars of the concert will be found in our advertising columns. STRANGE'S A.l. Crystal LAMP OIL in barrels or drums delivered free.—Sole agent, J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55, Bridge St., Warrington.—Advt. Junior Liberal Association, There was a good attendance at the weedy meeting of the above Association which was held on Monday evening in the Liberal Association Rooms, Bewsey- , street. The proceedings were of an impromptu character. Several political questions were thoroughly discussed. Election Expenses The following returns of election expenses have been banded in :—Councillor Ashcroft, i',l3 10s. 3d. ; Councillor Sankey, 12s. 3d. ; Councillor Wilson, £3l 17s. 6d. ; Councillor Nield, £2 ss. ; Councillor Barton, 17s. ; Mr. James Dodds, 2.32 is. 52. ; Mr. W. McNeil Sloane, i',l9 Os. 9d. The Rev. 1 Hirst.

_ The Lord Chancellor has offered the pleasantly situated Vicarage of Corse, six miles from Gloucester, to the Rev. J. Hirst, the Secretary of the Liverpool Diocesan Branch of the Church of England Temper- ance Society. We understand that Mr. Hirst, after visiting the parish, and making enquiries, has with much regret declined the offer as he considers that the opportunities for usefulneSs would not be sufficient. The amount of the cost of the dilapidations on the house and the glebe which he would have had to pay would also be too great. Warrington Ragged School. The limelight service on Sunday evening at the above place was conducted by Mr. Joseph Owen. The scenes from the New Testament were greatly enjoyed. On Monday evening a lantern lecture entitled, " Two months with my camera in India,"attracted an audience of about 450 pe Teens. Two illustrated songs " Killarney "and " On the banks of Allan Water " were sweetly sung by Miss Hipkiss. Master Pearce was the accompanist. The lantern was manipulated by Mr. Frank Owen at each service. Cycling Club Smoker. The coming of winter does not in any way abate the activity of the members of the Warrington Cycling Club, and some of the most enjoyable functions in connection with the club are the periodical smokers which are held daring the close season at the Patten Arms Hotel. The first of these was held on Thursday night, and attracted a large attendance, Mr. George Bowman presiding. Those present entered heartily into the proceedings, which were of a convivial nature, and a very pleasant evening was spent. Songs, , were given by Messrs. W. A. Clay, F. Fieldhouse, J. Willett, L. Hassall, G. Gough, and Alfred Grounds. Mr. T. R. Ford acted as accompanist. PuBLIC BENEFIT.—IINDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Advt. Licensing Change. On Tuesday, at the Borough Police Court, Mr. Steel referred to an application made by him a week ago for the transfer to Florence Jones of the off-licence, 223, Winwick-road. The Bench, in adjourning the applica- tion at that time, held that Miss Jones, who was 20 years of age, was too young, and it was suggested some older person should hold the licence for a time. Messrs. Peter Walker and Sons, Limited, the owners of the house, had had a large number of applications for the licence, but had been exceedingly kind to the family. and were desirous to help them. Miss Jones's grandfather, Mr. William Jones, a man of excellent character, had now come forward, and was prepared to bold the licence for a time.—Temporary authority was granted accordingly. PUBLIC BENEFIT, UNDER THE CLOCK Ton BEST BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Advt. Taxation of Land Values A meeting of the Warrington branch of the English League for the Taxation of Land Values was held on Friday in Gregory's Cafe. The Secretary gave a short explanation of the effects a tax on land values would have, and the justice as compared with the present injustice of taxation. In the discussion the question of justice in regard to the case of a recent purchase was raised and it was pointed out that Henry George had dealt with this point in the masterly chapter : "The great great grandson of Captain Kidd "in his book, " The Irish Land Question," in which he says that sale of a stolen article does not give any rightful claim to ownership. But apart from the question of justice, the small landowner who bought his land recently with well-earned money would not lose anything if he was working at all, since wages and profit in trading would rise to such an extent that be would be amply repaid for a possible small loss in rents.

LADIES' BEST GLACE BOOTS AND SHOES, UNDER THE CLOCK, BRIDGE-STREET.—Advt. TABLE, FLOOR, AND HANGING LAMPS in large variety. Latest patterns.—J. S. GARLAND, Iron- monger, Bridge st., Warrington.—Advt. Drank Carbolic Acid. Mr. Brighouse held an inquest at the Police Station on Tuesday evening , touching the death of Thomas Cooper, aged 73, a retired ironworker, who resided at 143, Longford-street, Warrington. Mrs. Cooper said at 12.45 on Tuesday her husband, after having par- taken of a light dinner, went to bed, saying he did not feel very well. At twenty to four she went to see how he was going on, but failed to rouse him. She sent for Dr. Ferguson, who pronounced life extinct. For several months her husband had complained of severe pains in the head, but he had never threatened to commit suicide. Before he retired to bed on Sunday he placed his hands to his head and remarked " I shall go mad."—Dr. Ferguson said a bottle con- taining carbolic acid was found under a chair in deceased's bedroom. Ho made a post-mortem examina- tion of the body and 'found it contained sufficient carbolic acid to kill two or three people—Mrs. Cooper said the carbolic acid had been kept in a shed in the yard for disinfecting purposes. She last saw it there about five weeks ago.—.A. verdict of " Suicide during temporary insanity" was retured. UNDER TILL CLoCB for Good BOOTS. Advt.—

div.head: PHASES OF THE CO-OPERATIVE MOVEMENT.
div.p: PHASES OF THE CO-OPERATIVE MOVEMENT.
LECTURE AT WARRINGTON. The Education Committee of the Warrington Co-opera- tive Society successfully launched a new departure on Thursday when the first of a series of lectures .was
delivered in in the Society's hall, Sankey-street. There was a large attendance over which Mr. Linnieus

Greening p-resided. The CHAD:max in a course of a brief address said the Co-operative movement was,he was sure, cap Vele of great development for the good of the community. Their Educational Committee was movinc, in the right direction for it was on this section that the future
success of the movement depended. He hada profound admiration for the Lecturer and the noble work be was

—.— doing not only in the Co-operative line but amongst the poor in the slums of London. The Co-operative movement began a long, long time ago. When men were young on the face of the earth, they co-operated together to fight agains:-. the great beasts of the field, it was then they triumphed in the fight and took a step forward and inward in the struggle for existence. This signal victory, paved the way for still further rapid developments, and now they had arrived at what he called the second stage in the

co-operative movement. A time when they were able to pay their members a substantial dividead, but even this was not the resting place. That success had encouraged thrift amongst thousands. The next upward co-operative movement was to be in the direction of the mental and social conditions of the people and this would be the most important of all. It was a natural sequence to all that had gone before, and now was the time to give a helping hand to forward the uplifting of the race to higher and better things. They could not measure in £ s. d. the 'flood that the new.3rooms, the payment of technical fees for thilp poor children, giving the hall free of charge, to Extension Lectures, and the work the Education Committee was doing but they might be quite sure that their efforts ,yould sooner or later bear good results and be to the - ?vantage of our native town. All thae expenditure of labour and money was a very wise and unselfish proceeding for it gave the young people a chance to prepare for the keen fight in the struggle amongst nations. He knew the difficulties, the disappointments that one met in that connection. but even in the face of such odds, the trouble and anxieties should count as nothing, when they saw, as we do from time to time,here and there, some who have taken advantage of their opportunities and become helpers and leaders in the mighty struggle, against the apathy, the back sliding and vice of poor humanity. He was delighted to know that the committees of nearly all the Co-operative Societies were moving in that direction, it was one of the good signs of the present day. It was indeed time to teach men that there was a higher ideal than making money, that it was their duty to he good citizens and their duty also to take an intelligent view and to work out the gr( Lt social and other problems that faced them in all directions in the present day. (Applause.) Mr. Greening concluded by speaking in praise of the Beautiful Warrington Society Mr. OWEN GREENING, of London, and formerly of Warrington, who had a hearty reception, delivered an interesting address on Phases of the Co-operative Movement." The Co-operative Society, he said, impressed itself upon him by reason of its power. In Warrington they were still flourishing in a material sense but, in spite of the establishment of an Educa- tional Committee, which he welcomed as one of the grandest steps the Society had taken, he felt there was something to say of the great possibilities before them. In Warrington their membership was such that it affected some 40,000 of the population, their average profit was 33 1-3 per cent, on the share capital—this was the average profit of the whole of the Societies in the country. If they could get the whole of the co-opera- tors of the country under the influence of the Co-operative Educational Committees, and get co-opera- tion into the hearts of the men and women of the country, and induce them to allow their money to accumulate, they could in a few years wipe off the national debt. Mr. Greening proceeded to illus- trate the immense power which the co-operators would be ableto sway if there was complete combination. They had power to accomplish great things and the first great thing they had to do was to abolish poverty. It was said that this was impossible. Two great political parties were scheming to bring about the abolition of poverty but he maintained that they could never save a man from poverty by machinery or by Act of Parliament. It could only be done by a system which WRS educa- tional from the beginning to the end. To do this it was necessary to take the children and give them a chance to learn and that ought to be the first duty of a great civilized Go vernment,and it was the duty of co-operative Educational Committee to supplement this. The. Co-operative Society was already performing a great service in this direction by teaching the working- man to make a week's wages pay for a week's sustenance and the next thing it became educational by inducing an extension of vision for one week to a quarter. Mr. Greening proceeded to illustrate how the whole of Society was co-operative but defective. They wanted to make that co-operation effective and to redeem the people from poverty and bring them to a higher social level. (Hear, hear.) By co-operation they could make themselves employers in every workshop in the kingdom and that was what they wanted to see—work- people partners with their employers. He was not preaching spoliation or confiscation. The employers would not be poorer than at present but would be better off. The employer would take a certain percentage on his interest and the balance of profit would go in dividends to the workers. This would result in a more harmonious working than at present and there would be an increase in the products of capital and labour by reason of the fusion of the two. They had to make the people realise the power that was in them, and to appreciate that it lay in themselves to redeem themselves. Here in Warrington they ought to have a small co-operative workshop or a big one if they could enter into co-partnership with the employers. If they could not get the employers they could start a little works of their own. There were to-day in England 120 successr,l co-operative workshops, which were producing results which were wonderful. Another direction in which they had to work was that of recreation. There ought to be in that Hall every night some form or other of recrea- tion for the yonng people. Dancing and athletics were absolute necessities for boys and girls, but this recrr tion must be provided under proper conditions, and it could be done in the Co-operative Societies. Let the fathers and mothers be there. If this vere done they would find that the young people would grow up to look upon the Society as the centre of everything enjoyable and profitable, and the Society would become a blessing to the town and to the country round. (Applause). During the evening musical items were given by the Warrington Co-operative Male Voice Choir, wha under the conductorship of Mr. E. A. Trow, acquitted them- selves admirably. • Mr. J. Willett also sang ably.

Saturday Evening Popular Concert. There was again a crowded attendance at the Popular Penny Concert which was held on Saturday evening in the Bold-street School. The Rev. J. F. Matthews presided, and pointed out that there were two things in these days that seemed to him to afford an opportunity for a better cultivation nf domestic music. The first was the increase of popular con- certs, which meant a wider range of local artistes, and the second the establishment of colleges which encouraged musical examination. Here the Germans excelled, as they did in a great many other things. Domestic music was particularly cultivated amongst them ; hence the high standard of efficiency attained, and the very great number of musicians whose work was appreciated by the British public. The Volkshed was an illustration of the point. It was to be hoped that as the years went on, there would be a great increase in the cultivation of music in the homes of the people. (Applause). Songs were given in an able manner by Mrs. Randalls, Miss Fairhurst, Mr. J. Willett and Mr. E. Walker, as well as coon songs by Miss M. Davis. Messrs. Crosfield's Quartette Party were in attendance, and gave several well rendered selections. The Padete Juvenile Trio were warmly applauded, and received an encore. Mr. H. Roberts was the humorist, and created roars of laughter with his funny sayings. The programme, which was iii every way an excellent one, was arranged by Mr. T, Brough.
The Examiner, Saturday, November 24, 1906.

the cook-room tent, and Graham himself supervised the dinner that night, in order, he explained somewhat apologetically, that I might not suffer from his conception of duty. "It was two days after this, and we had shifted camp fifteen miles, when, having occasion to go into Graham's tent after dark, I stumbled over someone sitting among the corner tent pegs. It was the grandpaps, of the white cock, and he explained to ma in his lingo—for he was one of the jungle people—that he had come in exchange for that precious bird. One life or another mattered little. Grim sahib had spared the child's heart's joy, which was now living with him in the maternal mansion. There being, therefore, no necessity for the occupation of hatching eggs, he, Bonder—yea! of a surety, it was the same name as that of the monkey people—had come to do service to the linzoors instead of the white cock. "That was absolutely all I could get out of him. So for days and weeks he followed us. He was useful in his way. especially to Graham. who had a

div.head: lvolnlnSni• ThE'SKELETON TREE.
div.p: lvolnlnSni• ThE'SKELETON TREE.

pautow not only for sport but for all sorts of odd .knowledge." I remember interrupting here that that was half the pleasure of new surroundings, to which my fellow-traveller replied drily that he had expected I would pay so, as I really reminded him very much of Graham.

"This passion of his, however, led him into being a bit reckless, and as the hot,weather came on he began to get touched up by fever. Still, he 'continued working-during the off-days, and seemed Jittle the worse, until one evening when he went to bed with the elvers after a leopard hunt. Then Md Bunder crept over to my tent. "Grim sahib must go home across the black water at once, Huzoor, he said, quietly, 'or his bones will whiten the jungle. He has seen the Skeletlan Tree.'

"That was, in essence, all he had to say, though his explanations were lengthy. It was simply a Skeleton Tree, and it was always seen where fire lingers met; but those who saw it became skeletons in the jungle before long unless they possessed a certain talisman. There were such talismans Among the hill tribes, and those who fell sick of fever always wore one if they could compass it. that was not often, since they were rare. He himself had one, but what use was it when life, from old age, had become no more worth than white cock's ? So his .grandson wore it • wore it Is lie fed the joy of his heart peacefully in the incestral home ;_thanks to Grim sahib 1

"But how 'clo you know he saw the tree? ' isked. 'lt was when we had crawled up nigh the -nd of a dip, Huzoor, ' replied Bonder. 'He (asked up and said: "What's that?" And when I isked him what he had seen, he said: "It is gone. It must have been that stunted tree. But it looked like a skeleton, and there were lire fingers round So I knew. Send him home, Huzoor, away 'mom its power, or his bones will whiten the jungle.' "During the following days I really began— . ;hough I'm not an imaginative chap—to feel -a bit peer about things. Graham couldn't shake off ais fever, and more than once when he was delirious in the evenings he'would startle me by laying: 'What's that ? But he would laugh the next moment, and add: 'Only a tree, of course; it was the light.' "There was bo doctor within miles.; and, .3esides, it was not really such a bad case as all hat. At least it didn't seem so to me or to arallain himself. Only to old Bonder, who became uiie a nuisance with his warnings, so that I was glad when, after a confused rigmarole about white :ocks tine sacrifices, he disappeared one day and was seen no more, partly, perhaps, because we moved back to a higher camp in the hope of , ?seeping the malaria. "But we didn't. Graham grew appreciably worse. He was fairly scell by day; it was at night that the fever seemed to grip him. I used to sit, up with him till twelve or one o'clock, and then turn in till about dawn when the servants had orders to call me, and I would go over and see after him "But one day, or rather night, it was still quite lark when my bearer roused me with his persistent drone of saheeb, saheeb ! ' and I knew in an instant something was wrong. Graham, shortly after I left him, had got out of bed, dressed himself in his shikar clothes, taken his gun, and gone from the camp. His bearer, a lad whom he had promoted to the place in one of his impulsive zenerous fits of revolt against things unjustifiable, had failed to take alarm until his master's prolonged absence had made him seek and rouse my man. The latter was full of apologies ; but what else, he pro- tested, could be expected of babes and sucklings promoted out of due season? The babe and suckling, meanwhile, was blubbering incoherently and assert- ing that he was not to blame. The sahib had called for Bonder and Bunder had come; and they had gone off together. "'Bonder ? ' I exclaimed. 'lmpossible! He hasn't been near the camp for days. Did anyone .Ise see him ? ' But no one had. And as there was no time to be lost in inquiries I dismissed the idea as an attempt on the boy's part to relieve himself from responsibility, and organised the whole camp into a search party. "It was a last quarter moon, and I shall never Forget the eeriness of that long, fruitless search. At first I kept, calling: 'Graham, Graham!' but after a time I felt this to be useless, and that he must either be unconscious, or delirious, or determined to keep out of our way. So I pushed an and on in silence, through the bushes and bents, expecting the worst. But after all it was the best.. We found him at dawn lying under one of those 4t unted trees fast asleep. So sound asleep that he did not wake when we cairied him back to camp on a litter of boughs. So sound that it was not until the afternoon, when he stirred and asked for beef- tea, that I discovered he wore round his neck a plaited cord of dirty.red silk with a small bag attached to it. "How did that come there ? ' he asked, drowsily, putting his hand up to feel it. How, indeed? He could never explain; and the bag held nothing but a bit of blank paper folded into four. He took the thing to England with him when he went home on sick leave the next month, and so far as I know is no wiser than he was then as to how it came round his neck."
Here my fellow-traveller paused, as a whistle from the engine told we were pulling up again. "Well," I said, a trifle plaintively, "but why should not I "

"This is my station," he replied, beginning to, gather his bedding together, "so I must hurry up. That was ten years ago. Two years after that I had to come over the same ground, doing the alignment. And just about the very spot where I found Graham—l believe under the very same tree —I came across the skeleton of an old bandy- legged, .bandy-armed mn. It may have been Bunder, it may not; but "—he was already getting out on to the deserted little platform at which we had drawn up—"if I were you I would not— Hare stationmaster, get out my things, will you?"

A minute after we were steaming' on again, 'taming him behind, a quaint figure in his striped sleeping-suit against the background of another arched oven with n bottle-gourd growing over. it. "Unless you have," came his voice, "a white cock to sacrifice to---" I could hear no more.

Whether the story he told me would have made me think twice before tempting malaria in the jungles Ido not know ; for when I reached the place whence I had intended starting I found at telegram which recalled me to England. I have not been in India since. But I never think of that railway journey without seeing some quaint visions. As for my fellow-traveller whom I left in the wilderness also in his striped sleeping-suit, I some.: times wonder if he was romancing or not. There is no reason why he should have been, for India holds many Bunders. It also holds Skeleton Trees, as anyone can see who who travels from Bhopal to Bandskui.
[THE END.

div.head: GRAIVIMAR SCHOOL SCHOLARSHIPS.
div.p: GRAIVIMAR SCHOOL SCHOLARSHIPS.
Means and Merits to be Considered.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Education Committee was held at the Town Hall on Monday evening under the presidency of Alderman Bennett. There were also present :—The Mayor (Aderman Smethurst), Alderman Evans, Councillors Ellison,Lord, Wilkinson, Toole, Pemberton, Cunnington, Ball, Evans, Sankey,Dr. Joseph, and Barton,the Revs. Canon Morley Stevenson, James Davies, John Yonge, and Neville Wilson, Miss Williams, Messrs. C. E. Parker, R. T. Fairclough, A. J. Jolley, H. Roberts, E. Plinston, G. Walker, and J. Moore Murray (secretary and director). At the commencement of the meeting the chairman congratulated the Res. Father Wilson on his restoration to health and welcomed Councillor Toole as a new member of the Committee. He also congratulated Councillor Lord on his re-appointment for a further three years.
THE BEAMDNT SCHOOL. BOARD OF EDUCATION CANNOT CONSENT TO .FEES.

At a meeting of the Finance Committee a letter was submitted from the Board of Education, stating that,s.s at present advised, they could not consent to the charge of fees at the Beamont Council School, and the com- mittee gave instructions for a reply to be sent to the Board with a view to their re-consideration of the request.

div.head: SCHOOL KEEPER.
div.p: THE SCHOOL KEEPER.

It was resolved that the salary of the keeper of the school be at the rate of .£lO4 per annum ; that be be required to live in the house attached to the school, and to pay ss. a week rent to the Committee, he to bear the cost of lighting and heating the house, but the com- mittee to pay the rates and taves; and that the managers of the school be authorised to obtain applications for the post, and be requested to consider the same and to recommend a candidate to the committee for appoint- ment after specially considering the claims of any of the existing staff of school keepers who may apply for the post. Mr. JOLLEY moved the adoption of the minutes and said the matter nf the school fees at the Beamont school was still under discussion between the committee and the Board of Education. With regard to the appoint- ment of school keeper, the Finance Committee fixed, in accordance with Ow regulation, the remuneration to be paid. The actual appointment rested with the managers but he might individually express the hope that they would both in the appointment of teachers and of the school keeper, bear in mind that there was a consider- able staff of teachers and school keepers working in the town, many of whom were worthy of promotion, and if the managers sele-ted anyone from the existing staff they would be setting up a very good precedent for the future administration of educational matters. _ _ . _

Councillor WILKINSON seconded, and said the managers had taken up the point mentioned by Mr. Jollev.They could not show undue preference towards the existing staff of school keepers, but their merits would be considered, and if any good man amongst them applied he would no doubt get promotion. Councillor LORD said that all things being equal. if they had two applicants for the post of school keeper they would certainly prefer their own townsman. PLINSTON asked for information as to the number of hours to be worked by Miss Ellen Litchfield who had been appointed cleaner in the Ilicondary school at a weekly wage of 7s. 6d. He also asked whether the committee had fully considered the remuneration to be paid to the catetaker at the Beamont school. He believed that in the new building there would he about 30 rooms and 40 fire grates. Considering the duties, he hardly thought 355. per week was sufficient. The DIRECTOR said Miss Litchfield would have to work thirty hours per week. Mr. JOLLEY said the Finance Committee went care- fully into the matter of remunerating the school keeper at the Beamont school. They took into consideration the nature of the plan of the building and the whole of the duties, and decided that £lO4 per annum was a fair and reasonable sum. The test would be the number of replies received when the vacancy was advertised. The CHAIRMAN srid he believed that preferential treatment of local applicants, everything else being equal, would be acceptable to the town. The minutes were approved. WARRINGTON GRAMMAR SCHOOL. THE SCHOLARSHIP QUESTION.

The School Management Committee reported that a letter having been submitted from the governors of the Warrington Grammar School, in reference to the award of the Council scholarships tendale at that school, it was resolved that the offer of the Governors to grant four such scholarships neat year be accepted ; but they be reminded that, should the number of pupils in the school warrant it, the committee will expect the governors to grant additional Council scholarships, over and above the four above-mentioned, until the total number of scholarships equals 20 per cent. of the num- ber of pupils then in the school, in accordance with the terms. of Resolution No. C 1210.

In reference to the regulations governing the award of these scholarships, the committee decided (a) to adhere to the Ist August as the date from which the admission age shall be reckoned, so as not to interfere with the eligibility of some boys who might wish to compete for the scholarships ; (b) to retain the paragraph requiring parents of success- ful candidates to satisfy the committee that that they are entitled by their circumstances to assistance in the education of their children ; and (c) to alter the date up to which applications may be received from the 30th to the Ist June, in accordance with the request of the governors.

To THE BEST OF NIICES AND NIPHIV/S, As I am writing this, the rain is simply coming down as it likes; the last two or three days nothing but rain, rain, rain. Oh, it is depressing( So you must not expect a very bright letter this week. , Talking of rain, do any of you know what the folks in ficotland do when it rains I I shall not tell you now, but will reserve it until next week. Well, I suppose meet of you are eager to know the winners of this week's prizes. They are little contributors A—. B—. (who unfortunately omitted the full name, but fortunately for him or her, has attached the address), and Eva Sylvester. The first for sending in the Square Word Puzzle and a tale entitled, "Stealing a Dog." Eva gains the other prize for a set of verses entitled, "Dainty." To each, of these successful relations the postman will bring a lovely box of Chocolates. Well, how did the fireworks go off—with a bang, as usual. I expect Guy Fawkes ap- peals to some of you more so than our other old friend, Santa Claus; or, as our American friends call Lim, Kris Kringle. Well, he'll soon be here now, so see that all your stockings have a jolly big hole in them—at the top, I mean. Well, my dear Children no more this week from • 2 UNCLE NED.
Dear Uncle Ned,—l am sending you the answers to the puz,zles in the " Examiner " dated November 3.
SQUARE WORD. CAT ADO TOM CHARADE. Car—pet Carpet. ACROSTICS. Money. A Gift. Received. Spent. MARS. I remain, your loving niece, Dom BOND. (Age, 8 years.)

Dear Uncle Ned,—l am writing to thank you for the lovely box 0 chocolates you have so k;ndly sent me for gaining a prize in the "rimlet Mat" competition. I only received it this morning. As it went to Littleham, near Exmouth, this caused come delay. I feel quite proud to think I have gained three prizes. I hope I shall be as (successful in the future. Again thanking you, I am, dear Uncle Ned, your lovink niece, OLIVE KINGDON.

Dear Uncle Ned,—Wishing to beeome a. new member of your league, I am sending you this story, hoping to Gee it later on printed in the " Children'c Corner." Hoping you are quite well, with lays from your affectionate niece, MAX SANDERS.
Dear Uncle Ned,—l hope you will. like this piece of poetry. It is entitled—" Jellyboy'e Christaize." Hoping you are in the beet of health, I remain, your loving niece,
ELSIE HORRILL.

JOLLYBOY'S CHRISTMAS. Oh, Christmas ,is blithesome and jolly, It ousts "dumps" and dull melancholy, Not a sorrow or care, And I have my fair share, But is off at the sight of the holly. It's good-bye to business and worry, So one cannot help but be merry, hurra,l7.• for home joys, v" With the girls and the boys, And the little mites all in a flurry. Though old, Yet I don't mind, the weather, It max...rain, snow, and Lail, all together, I care lilt a: pin,

- _ For we're jolly within, And illy fltrL as light as a feather. If it's just in the humour it freezes, .Then I feel in such spirits, it eases, My mind, then I take, A dear friend's hand to shake, To give it a few extra squeezes. My efforts at skating are 'humble. And my bones are a bit apt to grumble, But I run with the rest,

And can slide with the best, And how we all laugh when I tumble! When the bell rings the hour for dining, For turkey and pudding we're pining, So I cry, "Who'll be first?" And away we all burst, Till my face beats the silver for shining. And what can be brighter or better, Than a nice Christmas card or a letter? Oh, it makes my heart heave, Ev'ry gift I receive, •And I feel Pm to friendship a debtor. I wish you the joys of the selson, If you want to be glad you'll find reason, For Christmastide brings Such a troop of good things, To be doleful or dull b rank treason.
lear Uncle Ned, I am sending you an of puzzles, besides a story, which I gain a prize.
om your affectionate nephew, le A—.
STEALING A DOG.
.learly a hundred years ago, a very et dog lived in Manchester. It was a !al rspaniel, and its master loved it so much -
[ever lack
tbai

te would not sell it. He would hide money under a stone, or in the earth, and send the dog back several miles to fetch it. He would point out a duck on a pond, or wild birds on a river, and the dog would bring them home when his master called for them. One day a stranger °aught the dog, took it into a canal boat, tied it fast, and carried it to London. He sold it to a gentleman in London, sand left it there, while he returned in his boat to Man- chester. The dog soon ran away from h'e new master, walked through London and Maccles- field to Manchesster. He reached his old home one cold, wet night in winter. He was thin, lame, and tired, but his old master was glad to eee him. Some days After he went with his old master to an inn in the neighbourhood.' A sturdy, surly-looking man stood at the bar as they went in. The dog flew at the strarkier's throat. It tore his waistcoat, and we killed him, if its master had not t , He was the thief who had etolen the C.og and carried it to London.
