div.head: AUTOBIOGRAPHY 'OP A. PENNY,
div.p: AUTOBIOGRAPHY 'OP A. PENNY,

T was born in 1892, in a large place called a Mint. Then I was of a bright, shiny Ce but as years sped on I became very dull. When I left the Mint, accompanied by many other coins; I was given to a shop-girl, with put me in a drawer. Oh it was dark in that draiv?,:. and I was exceedingly glad when the s.cii•-:*.l took. me out. She gave me to a little boy, wi,•, chuckled with glee when he saw that I was a shiny colour. He held me fait unt.l it reached home, for he was afraid of losing me. He then plated me in a large money-box. I soon became acquainted with the other coins, and I heard them say to one another, "What a bright colour he is.", I felt -very proud when I heard this remark. ""About a week after I been in my new home, a little .girl ran room, and opened the box. In doing let it fall, and all the coins fell out on ;!. • •:. She stooped down, and picked us Up. shut the box and went out. Soon after, tlie 13y took me out, and, going for a penknife, he 7,". ve me to a lady in exchange for the/ penknife. The Lady, as she was goinjg home, let' me fall into the gutter. I laid there for a few mil-olio; •i• before rain began to fall on me. The di. became heavier and heavier, and almost' mida me quake with fear. However, it soon lieciime fine, and I became overcome with joy when a boy hurried • past. He turned hack, and, stirL.p- ing down, picked me up. When he reached home, he placed me in his purse. I cannot tell you what my adventures are for the future, because he is saving his money to buy some large thing.
C. CALLING.

Dear Uncle Ned,—l am going to desciibe to i'ou the interesting places of Northam. One of the interesting places is Bone hill. It is named Bone hill because a number of English and Danes were buried there. In ithe middle of Bone hill is a flagstaff, which was erected in memory of our good Queen Victoria. All around Bone-hill are seats. Another intcrc3t- ing place is Bloody Corner, where King Alfred the Great killed King Hubba, the Dane, in a bloody retreat. There is a stone put there in memory of the event, and bn the stone is writ- ten, "Stop, stranger, stop. Near this spot lies King Hubba, the Dane, who was slain by Kinf; Alfred the Great in a bloody retreat." And another interesting place is Borrough Fartn, where Amyas Lee was born.

mine. Said Archy, "I've got it, so there!" Said Bobby, "Now let us divide in lout parts, • And each of us boys have a share." "No, no!" shouted Tommy; "I'll have it myself." Said Peter, "I want it, I say." Said Archy, " l've got it, and I'll have it all; I won't give a morsel away." Then Tommy he snitched it, and Peter he I fought ('Tis sad and distressing to tell); And Archy held on with his might and his

main, Till out front his fingers it fell. Away from the quarrelsome urchins it flew, And then down a green little hill; The apple it rolled, and rolled, and rolled As though it would never be still. A lazy old cow was cropping the grass, And switching her tail at the flies; When all of a sudden the apple rolled down, And stopped just in front of her eyes. She gave but a bite and a swallow or two,
That apple was seen no more. "I wish," whimpered Archy, and Peter, and Tom, "We'd kept it, and cut it in four." W. CLARKE.

Dockyard Founder's Martyrdom to Plies and how it was Ended ;3y Bi!s Beans •

div.head: FREE CHURCHES.
div.p: FREE CHURCHES.
THE FREE CHTIRC.HES AND THE LORDS.

There is only one feeling among the Free Churches on the Question of the action of -the House of Lords td the Government's Educa- tion Bill--that is oneof intense indignation anti determination to resist. Four years ago, when 'Mr. Balfour introduced his educational measure, a storm of indignation at once swept through the Free Churches. Now, in spite of the agitations, distraints, imprisonments, and the General Election, which so em- phatically recorded the decisio,a of the country against Mr. Balfour and his policy, the Lords have !J",:s.Cll shaping the Government's measure t.u. heir liking, in utter disregard of history or the facts of the situation., More than this, they have been introducing" into the measure proposals which not even Mr. Balfour at the height of his power would have dared to bring into the House of Commons. N:hurally, when these things became known immediate action had to be taken. The National Free Church Council, which has fought the battle so per- sistently during these years, at once took the matter up. For the first time in its history their full, assembly was specially summoned, and all the representatives who had taken part in the last annual meeting were invited to a Conference in London'. In spite of very short notice, representatiyes were present from all parts of the country, and united with one voice in indignantly repudiating the action of the House of Lords, and calling on the Government to resist the same. The Rev. Thomas Law states that the feeling in the country was so strong. that had the National Council refused to act, their friends in the country would have broken up the organisa- tion. Of course, there was never any re- luctance on the part of the National Council Executive. This great gathering made a pro- found impression, and Free Churchmen were relieved and. delighted to have Mr. Birrell's assurance that the Government would not accept the amendments of the House of Lords.

div.head: C:IPSY SMITH IN AMERICA.
div.p: C:IPSY SMITH IN AMERICA.

Gipsy Smith the well-known missioner of the. National Smith, Church Council, is at pre- sent engaged on an Evangelistic tour in the United States. He ,started in New York, conducting missions at different centres, and, in Spite of the .intense excitement consequent on the elections, the buildings in which he spoke were packed with crowds anxious to hear the Gospel meKage. Gipsy Smith has now started a promising in Boston. In a recent communication to the Rev. Thomas Low he says :--I am received everywhere with the utmost affection. The missions in this city-began with a banquet of 500 ministers and. laymen, andll meet a United Ministers' meeting on Monday next. I hope for great things from these gatherings. The ministers of all Churches seem most Anxious to welcome an evangelistic movement under wise leader- ship. The results are growing daily. It is a joy to know we ai:e not forgotten, and it is a sweet thought to me to feel my own people are keeping me and this great work constantly before the Throne of Grace."
THE CONGO SCANDALS.

The news of the Congo atrocities is gradu- ally permeating the conscience of the country. The news of the doings of the officials of the Congo Free State reveal an almost incredible state of affairs. The mutilations, outrages, massacres, seem to be part of the ordinary youtine for gathering rubber. Many of the stories of cruelty and wickedness will not sear repetition. The feeling, of the Churches en this matter is slowly rising, and it will not be surprising if we are soon face to face with a great agitation on the question. The Executive of the National Free Church Coun- cil had the matter under consideration, and a letter has been sent to each of the local councils urging them to take action. Of course this is more than a Free Church matter, and co-operation with other bodies is recom- mended. The best course to be adopted is to approach local mayors to arrange town's meet- ings. There is urgent need for action on the part of our Government, kind under existing treaties action can be taken without fear of those complications which are always threat- ened when interference in Turkish affairs, for instance, is urged. But, if this action is to be taken, the Government must have at its back a strong national feeling. This the Free Churches can help to create. •

CHURCH MUSIC. tose interested in • the music of our Churches will by this time be perusing with interest the " Free Church Council Hymnal," which the National Free Church Council has just issued. This, of course, is an entirely new publication; and has been prepared by a special committee of the National Council, under the able editorship of the Rev. S. F. Most of those who have had to do with the organisation of large United Miss;ons and other gatherings have felt the need of a ser- viceable collection of hymns, not too large for public distribution, but extensive enough for freedom of choice. This new collection, con- taining 283 pieces, combines the hest worship hymns of the Church with the evangelistic hymns specially required for mission work. Those interested in Free Church . hymnology should get a prospectus of this new publica- tion from the National Council's Publication Department, Memorial Hall, E.C.
MISSIONARY CONFERENCE.

In pursuance of its .object of creating midi- sionary enthusiasm among the Free Churches, the Missionary Committee of the National Council,has arranged for Dr. Horton to con- duct a series of Missionary Conferences in different parts of the country. The first of these was at Bristol on November 20, and the arrangements included an afternoon confer- ence, public tea, and a public meeting. Other conferences are to be held at East Dereham for East Anglia, and Hull for the Yorkshire districts.

div.head: FORTHCOMING MEETINGS.
div.p: FORTHCOMING MEETINGS.
Preparations are already in progress for the annual meetings of the National Free Church nimneil which are to be held at Lee..l

March -4 to 7 iticw. lif course the organisinz of such a series of gatherings as these means an immense amount of labour. Local com- mittees have already been formed at Leeds, and are giving careful consideration to the arrangements. The delegates who will as- semble there next March may be sure of a real Yorkshire welcome. The most difficult task of the local committee is always the pro- vision of hospitality. Beds have to be pro- vided for more than a thousand visitors, and in a case like this delay until the last moment trebles the work. Local Free Church Councils are being urged to appoint their representa- tives immediately.
SOME SPECIAL FEATURES.

Already it is intimated that practically all the prominent Free Church leaders will be present at Leeds in March, (Ind that a most interesting and important programme is cer- tain. One of the most interesting features will be the presence of General Booth. It is also announced that an address is to be given by Sir Oliver Lodge. Sir Oliver's great reputation as a scientist and a Christian should ensure his good reception.

match was A, H. Rathbone, who playing centre half, fairly came out of his shell, so much so that it has been thought advisable to retain him in the premier eleven. if he will maintain this form, and swing the ball about from wing to wing, he should prove a good acquisition. Praise must also be given to H. W. Guest, who played a good sound game. R. Hallows at back was also in good form, whilst the forwards reproduced the form shown against Northern. It was a pleasure to see Dolan play so well, as he has been rather off colour lately, whilst W. Richardson has again found his shooting form. Of course Banks played well ;he must obtain recognition soon from the county selection com- mittee. The goals for Stockton Heath, were scored by W. Richardson 2, W. H. Banks 1, S. Baxter 1.

The second eleven did not carry out their intention of putting Formby second" through it," in fact they were defeated 3-1, though leadihg at half time and hav- ing the wind at their backs in the second portion of the game. C. W. Walker again showed good form, and is Improving every match.

Workmen's Cottages Wanted at Walton. Sir,—Might I call your attention to the scarcity of workmen's cottages in the neighbourhood of Stag Bridge at a weekly rental of about 49. During the past three or four years several industries have sprung up in this neighbourhood and the workmen have to walk a couple of miles to their work for lack of suitable accommodation. There is plenty of land to be got along the Chester- road and it might be of some interest to the master builders of the Town to know this.—Yours truly, WORKMAN.

Warrington. November 22nd, 100 G. Paving In Padgate-lane. Sir,----Can you or any of your readers inform me why the crossings in Manchester-lane - beyond the Cemetery gates that have only been opened out a few months ago have already been paved, yet those in Padgiite-lane that have been opened from 15 to 20 years are not yet paved ? Can this be the truth about the Manchester- lane crossings being paved, that they lead to land belonging to a Corporation official?lt is time Councillor Duncan has a look at Padgate-lane on a wet day and sees what wants doing, and has a walk round some of our beautiful lakes. They don't help our Beautiful Warrington Society,but provide facilities for children to sail their boats and induce them to stay away from school. The one crossing by Councillor Duncan's window is the worst in the lot ; perhaps he cannot see it, or else it is too paltry for a Councillor's notice.—Yours 3;c., MUD DODGER.

div.head: The" Liberator" Relief Fund.
div.p: The" Liberator" Relief Fund.

Sir,—The aged and afflicted victims of the great "Liberator "Fraud have been largely indebted to a generous press for the valuable aid rendered from time to time in making known their pitiable condition, through being so cruelly robbed of their life-savings,— thereby enabling my Committee to raise the Relief Fund, mainly by advertisements and appeals through I the post, at the lowest possible cost. This fact emboldens me once again to crave the hospitality of your columns to answer a question which many friends of the'effort are just now asking, viz., as to whether the Fund will not soon be coming to a close? Two I sentences from the last Annual Report of the Executive Committee,—(a copy of which I shall be happy to send to anyone who writes for it), will I think be a sufficient reply. " The perpetrators of the great wrong that caused such widespread wretchedness in September, 1892, may have purged their crime in the eyes of the law, but its painful coasequences, in privation and hardship, must be still endured by many hundreds for several years to come, though, it is hoped, still mercifully assuaged by I the ministry of the Relief Fund. No fewer than 9001 victims who were upon the books of the Fund have passed to their eternal rest; but so many who only had temporary help at first, being older and entirely unable to work, are compelled now to seek permanent relief fromithe Fund, that there are still fully a thousand who are receiving regularly half-yearly grants." And whether many of these, the large majority of whom are widows and spinsters between 65 and 75 years of age, will have the great comfort of knowing that they will continue to receive this most welcome assist- ance, or may yet have to face the dreaded workhouse in despair, depends upon the further response of the generous public, to whom I am constrained to most earnestly appeal on behalf of my poor clients for another £lO,OOO. Sincerely thanking you in anticipation, on behalf of my Committee, Tam, yours faithfully. J. STOCKWELL WATTS, Secretary of the •• Liberator" Relief Fund. 16, Farrington-street, E.C. 17th November, 1906,

Pauper Labour. Sir,—The recent prosecution of a pauper painter, by the Board ef Guardians, for refusing to do work found for him and thus wilfully neglecting to maintain him- self whereby he became chargeable to the Union, has shown to the public the dangers of such a proceeding. The unfairness of such an action is beyond question. If it is possible to punish paupers for refusing to work for a mere pittance, what should be done with the people who employ them at a rate of wages which would probably not be offered to them,but for the very fact of their poverty and helplessness ? In this particular case, the cause of the man's discom- fiture proceeded from a sudden partial attack of charity on a member of the Board of Guardians. Now charity is a dangerous workmate. It is never satisfied and invariably expecting. It begins at home,sometimes;and,when it does,it ends there. And it is quite evident that the charity meted Out to the poor beggar in this case was lob-sided, or else the Magistrates would not have been troubled with him. And yet it was admitted by the Master of the Work- house that during the time the pauper had been in the " house " he had been very useful and had unquestion- ably saved the ratepayers a large amnunt of money. Strange that he should be found guilty of neglecting to maintain himself ! Your leacierette is funny, as usual, You say : "If we take a man off the road 'nod set him to painting the shop-front we shall not ask the Trades Council how much we ought to pay him even if he be an R.A. and his standard wage is Li an hour." Why, lathe name of commonsense, should you offer a man you take" off the road" less than the man who is your neighbour ! If he does the work as well, is he not entitled to the same remuneration ?—Yours truly, EDMUND OSBORNE. Padgate, 23rd November, 190 G. [With regard to the latter part of Mr. Osborne's latter we should like to add," in the name of commonsense that we should offer the man what we thought the job was worth and no more.—Ed. "EL"]

div.head: Rector and the Prayer Book.
div.p: The Rector and the Prayer Book.

Sir,—l am pleased the Rector received my criticism in such a kindly way, and that he has replied with such good feeling. I am by no means a lover of controversy, desiring to preserve the "unity of the spirit in the bond of peace" with all my brethren who are engaaed in. the sacred work of the Gospel. But perhaps I may be allowed a further word on this vexed question and may state at once that while Canon Willis's letter leaves no doubt as to his views and aims, it creates for me more difficulties than it explains. Like many another Protestant Churchman, my earliest religious impressions were received, and a considerable portion of my life was spent, in the very atmosphere of Ritual and doctrine which the Rector desires to see introduced into this town. Thus, I may claim to have more than a passing interest in the Liturgy which I have known and loved all my life. And while this magnificent monument of national piety has been, and still is, the scene of much bitter strife and con- tention, by reason of its doubtful forms of expression, yet the fact remains that very many sons of the English Church within and without its pale, have the strongest possible reasons for believing that there is something more behind all this discussion and conflict than either a diversity of discernment in the study of history, or the ignorance of the English language on the part of the Reformers of the lfith Century—and that " some- thing" they conceive to be a re-introduction of doctrine or practice which has no warrant from Holy Scripture and which is peculiar to that Church from which at the Reformation we were freed. Canon Willis says " the Protestant Revision of 1552 was in the main the utterance of foreign ecclesiastics who didinot understand the English language." Presumably he refers amongst others to Calvin,Alasco,Peter Martyr,and Bucer, who admittedly played an important part in its compilation. It must not be forgotten, hawever, that the two last named were especially invited by Arch- bishop Cranmer "that he might strengthen the Evangelical doctrine," and being eminent scholars were appointed Regius Professors of Divinity at Oxford and Cambridge respectively—sufficient testimony to their ability and soundness in teaching. Naturally the scholarly advice of the leading teachers of the Universi- ties was sought by the English Bishops and Divines during their work in committee 1550-1552. It may be true that, for them Latin Versions had to he prepared, but what of Crammer, Ridley, Latimer, Hooper and others, who not only endorsed their suggestions and doctrines, but went to the Stake in support of them ? It is difficult to believe these great and good men did not know the English Language, or had no sympathy with the purest traditions of the past. It is well known they represented much more than Papal supremacy. What an advance in education has been made since then ! And yet with the further light of 100 years, on language and doctrine, many of England's most learned divines from that day to this, have set their faces against any return to the lines of the first book of 1549 advocating only such things as can be found in the Word of God or be proved thereby. In my opinion, Sir, the Rector's reference to Cranmer is also liable to be misunderstood by many readers. It is a quotation from the Archbishop's famous challenge rude after the accession of Mary refuting the report that he " should set up the Mass at Canterbury " The book of 1552 had now become law in the English Church, and the fact that Cranmer couples Peter Martyr with himself in the challenge,the part the latter played in its construction is sufficient to show him to be referring to the Second Book as "more pure and according to God's Word than any that bath been used in England these thousand years." It is quite true Ido not read history as the Rector does and cannot but think it would be the gravest disaster cf modern times if a Revision on the lines of the first book ever became law in this coun- try. When the Revision comes, if it ever does, I pray it may be on the lines of that Pentecostal Protestantism which has made England what she is, and which gains and keeps for all her sons the liberty wherewith Christ bath made us free. However, the time has not arrived when men see eye to eye on these matters ; till then I trust we may do our work with singleness of purpose and with as little friction as possible.—Yours &c., FRANK VAUGHAN. Emmanuel Church, Warrington. November 24st, 1.901 i.

A USEFUL CAREER.
OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.

Services for Sunday. Wycliffe Congregational Church: Preacher, 10.30 and 6.30, Rev. J. Yonge. Evening subject A true Christian Knight "—lessons from the life of Sir George Williams, founder of the Y.M.C.A. Bold-street Wesleyan Church: Preachers, 10.30, Rev. S. Pitt; 6.30, Rev. E'. J. Gawne. Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church: Preachers, 10.30, Rev. J. Manning; 6.30, Rev. J. Gunnel. Baptist Church, Golborne-street : Preacher, Rev. L. Thomas, Openshaw. Subjects. 10.30, " Spiritual Photo- graphy" ; 6.30, " Self-respect and self-control." Latchford Baptist Church : preacher, Rev. J. F. Matthews ; subjects 10.30 "A Royal Priesthood," 6.30 "The Christian interpretation of sorrow." Confirmation Service.

A confirmation service was conducted at Holy Trinity Church on Monday afternoon, when 55 candi- dates-24 males and 31 females—from Holy Trinity Church and the Blue Coat School, were presented. The ceremony was performed by the Lord Bishop of Liverpool (Dr. Chavasse). The Bishop, in the course of a short address, said that they had come there that afternoon to give themselves to God, and God would give Him- self to them. He sincerely hope 1 that now they had been confirmed they would attend Holy Communion regularly. Presbyterian Sunday School Anniversary.

I The Sunday school anniversary was celebrated at St. John's on Sunday when the pulpit was occupied morning and evening, by the Rev. C. L. Stowe. There was a ' good attendance at each service. In the evening, Mr. Stowe chose for his text, "The crown wherewith his mother crowned him " (Songs of Solomon iii. 11). The preacher observed that George Herbert said "A good mother is worth a hundred schoolmasters," and the longer they lived the more convinced they became of the truth of that statement. If the parents were making 1 a religious diadem for their children they were sending out into the world men and women who could be trusted in the years to come. Special hymns and anthems were ; rendered, and Mr. J. W. Jowett, organist and choir- master, presided at the organ. Satisfactory collections were obtained in support of church and school funds

div.p: loud applause, and then proceeded to deal with ques- tions which poured upon him thick and fast. In reply to one question as to whether a man could not live on £1 a week in the country, Mr. Dunnico said it would certainly be easier to do so there, but they must not forget that seventy-seven per cent of the population were living in towns. In reply to another question, Mr. Dunnico said that possibly emigration might allevi- ate, but why should they send their best brain and muscle across the seas when this country under proper management could provide sufficient to keep double the present population?

div.head: Churchmen_ and Nonconformists
div.p: Churchmen_ and Nonconformists

The Rev. H. A. Lester, M.A., delivered a lecture under the auspices of the Warrington Church Society in St. Clement's Mission on Thursday evening on "The Church and Nonconformity." There was a large attend- ance and it was announced that letters regretting inability to be present had beea received from the Rev. ; John Yonge, the Rev. J. Manning and others. The Rector, who presided, said there were three things which he would like to say in regard to Nonconformity ; —three great things it seemed to him. First, Noncon- formity was modern. •It only dated from Post j Reformation times. It was not 350 years old. Could they seriously think that God would have left His Church without guidance for more than 1,500 years? He begged them to ask themselves seriously that question. Secondly, it was wasteful. What did it do? It was ' overlapping them at every point. Let him give an illustration. Their dear, kind good friend, Mr. Monks—he respected him very much—had recently started a Nursing Association in Warrington. What would he think if anybody should start an opposition Society to do the same work in the same area? So that Nonconformity, instead of uniting with the Church and helping them, formed opposing Societies. This was a great waste of energy. Thirdly, Nonconformity was very partial. They heard sometimes of men preaching the Gospel as they said in opposition to the Church—as if the Church were not preaching the Gospel. It was just there that he had a great fault to find with Dissent. To preach the Gospel did not mean the preaching of certain points. They were quite right to press strongly certain points, but they had got to teach the whole faith—the truth as it was in Jesus. To dwell upon some points and leave out the other points was not to his mind to preach the Gospel. The Rev. H. A. LESTER dealt at some length with the " evils and dangers " of disunion among Christians He condemned the spirit of aloofness shown on both sides, contended that" political Dissent" in which the Ireligious element seemed comparatively small led people sometimes to forget the real piety and devotion of a vast host of Dissenters, and said another evil was the hesitating policy which tended, to leave things in the hands of extremists and thus foster disruption. It must also be remembered that bigotry, obstinacy, ignorance and incapacity were not the exclusive posses- sions of Churchmen but were found sometimes among Dissenters. As tendencies towards unity be pointed out the realization of the need of unity among the Nonconformists as Was shown by the Congregational Union and Free Church Council ; the desire of many Nonconformist bodies for a common simple creed or rather the getting rid of the distinctive shibboleths which in trust deeds and other ways had done so much harm in stereotyping certain special beliefs which were not now so generally believed as essential—a desire which found utterance in the Free Church Catechism ; the abandonment of many outward tokens of separation from the Church such as the adoption of the word "church " instead of "chapel, " the free use of Gothic architecture and of some Church-like arrange- ments, the use of the organ and introduction of chanting, the occasional use of special forms of service. the religious observance of Christmas Day and Good Friday, and the adoption of a more clerical dress by ministers. Unity, continued the lecturer, must not be gained by the sacrifice of truth and the four main essentials which Churchmen were bound to maintain I were : The Catholic Creed and Scriptures, the belief in the visible Church founded by Christ, the belief in the two great sacraments, and the belief in and the maintenance of the Apostolic ministry. There could be no union with people who did not hold the great doctrines of the Holy Trinity and the Incarna tion. In the question of the Apostolic ministry lay tht greatest obstacle to re-union. Churchmen could noe regard the Apostolic ministry as a matter of slight importance and they could not endanger it by treating those who did not possess it as though they did. Mr. Lester enumerated a number of things for which the Church of England was indebted to Nonconformity,and on the other hand he maintained that the Church of England had been the cause of preserving the Pro- testanism of England from drifting into that excess of false doctrine and infidelity which had made such inroads on the Protestantism of the Continent. Con- tinuing, Mr. Lester urged his hearers to pray for re-union, to take advantage of all opportunities of co-operating with Nonconformists, to strive to know Nonconformists socially and personally as friends, and advocated the holding of conferences between Church- people and Nonconformists to discuss their difference in the spirit of love and prayer. The usual votes of thank l concluded the meeting.

div.head: BEAMONT SCHOOL. -- Application for a Loan for Street Paving.
div.p: THE BEAMONT SCHOOL. -- Application for a Loan for Street Paving.

Lieutenant-Colonel A. C. Smith, R.E., an inspector of the Local Government Board, held an inquiry at the Town Hall yesterday morning into the application of the Corporation for sanction to borrow £6,486 for Private Street Works. Mr. A. T. Hallaway (depnty town clerk) made the application on behalf of the Corporation and amongst those present were the Mayor (Alderman Smethurst), Alderman Tinnion (Chairman of the Paving and Sewerage Committee), Messrs. T. Longdin (borough surveyor), A. M. Ker (assistant surveyor), J. Fairhurst (borough treasurer), T. H. Spinks (assistant town clerk). Mr. Hallaway explained that the application was divided into two parts. The first related to the paving of the streets round the Beamont Soho A—Garner- street, O'Leary-street, Wilkinson-street, Richardson- street and Duncan-street. The time for making objections had expired, bnt none had been received. The second part of the application referred to Grafton- street, Windsor-street, and Lexden-street, but the time for receiving objections would not expire until December 12th. No objections were anticipated. A statement was presented showing that the indebted- ness of the borough amounted to £1,186,478, less £8,8" in sinking funds. The Borough Treasurer pointed out that the Council passed a resolution granting property owners seven years for the repayment of loans. The formation and paving of the streets took seven months and afterwards the apportionments had to be made, so that nearly I twelve months elapsed before the arrangements were completed. He would therefore be glad if the Board would allow the council eight years for the payment of loan as he could foresee that if only seven years were allowed there wonld at the expiration of that time be an instalment owing and the Board would probably have something to say about it. I Alderman Tinnion said he desired to emphasise the urgency of the work, particularly of that relating to the streets surrounding the Beamont schools. The building would be opened early in the new year. It had been built practically on green sod, and what were called streets were at present not fit for the passage of chil- dren, particularly in the winter months. The other streets were not quite so urgent, but still they required attention, and many property owners as well as tenants were anxious ftir the work to be pushed on. The Inspector said he would represent the urgency of the application to the Board.
There was no opposition and the inquiry closed.

Warringtonians Married in Canada. A very pleasing event was consummated at the residence of Mr. Stephen Benson, Neefawa, Manitoba. Canada, on Wednesday, October 17th, when Miss Amy Meredith Winstanley, daughttr of Mr. William Henry Winstanley, Rolleston-street, Warrington, was united in marriage to Mr. Thomas Irvine, of .Neefawa, formerly of Wallington. The ceremony took place at the • - 2.30 p.m in e presence of Mr. and Mr. Benson and .. family, Mrs. Bray, Miss Hutchinson, Mr. and Mrs. R 4. '"- Evans, of Rossall, near Blackpool, and Mr. W. J. Edwards, of Winsford, Cheshire. The Rev. Horace . Bray, KB., Rector of Ss. John's Church, Port Rowan, 4 ,- Ontario, officiated. The bride, who was unattended, ~' was given away by Mr. Benson, and looked very ; charming. J.` Although only a week in this country," says the report which appeared in the Neefawa local ' paper, "she has already made many friends by her - sweet expressions and pleasant manner. The groom is also deservedly popular." After the ceremony those present were most hospitably entertained at a delight- ful dinner by Mr. and Mrs. Benson. The presents were very numerous. Mr. Irvine, who left Warring- ton some seven months ago, was for some years with Mr. Charles Price, provision merchant, Market-gate, and on arriving at Neefawa, entered into partnership with Mr. Benson as dairy farmers, and is, as Ins many friends will be pleased to learn, carrying on a very ' successful business.

• STARS. Oh twinkling stars that glitter in the night How blest the beauty of your wonderous light How few have thought what winter nights would be If nought but daikness filled immensity. The lonely sun in endless space would shine With all the glory of His power divine The pale moon wander sadly on her way And earth be darkened at the close of day. When the new moon withholds her silvery light No heavenly orb would cheer us in the night When shortest days are wintery cold and drear Sad and deserted would the earth appear. • Unseen by day while here on earth we dwell Oh blessed stars what wondrous tales ye tell Forever looking on this world of strife I love to see ) ou watching o'er our life. • Gazing I feel the little that we know There may be worlds to which the dying go Unseen as stars amid the glare of day A brighter clime to which they pass away. 10h stirs, bright stars,so infinite sublime We yearn to live beyond the bounds of time So beautiful the universe that we Would worship God for all eternity. S. KENYON. November, 1906. GRANDMOTHER'S MINCEMEAT. This is the week in which most methodical cooks make their mincemeat. The writer, remembering her first" making " of mincemeat, which entailed a whole day's labour and resulted in some two stones of mince- meat (for a family of two !), counsels young wives not to venture upon too large an undertaking. Here is a delightful old-fashioned recipe which, if carefully followed, will produce just enough and not too much mincemeat for a small family. 41bs. of apples, pared, cored and minced. 151bs. of raisins, stoned and minced. 2 lbs. of beef suet,finely shred. 4 lbs. of dried currants. 1 lb. of castor sugar lb. candied peel,minced. on. salt. oz. finest mixed spice. The minced rinds of 4 lemons, the juice of two. ?, pint of sweet wine. -5, pint of brandy. Mix the whole well together, press into a deep pan and keep covered in a dry, cool place. CROSFIELDS v. SHIP CANAL COMPANY. A Cross Appeal. The respondents in the action, Crosfield and Sons Limited, Warrington, v. the Manchester Ship Cana Company, petitioned the Appeal Committee of the House of Lords to be allowed to lodge a cross appeal, although the time for lodging a cross appeal, by the standing orders, had expired. It may be remembered that this was an appeal on the merits of the controversy between the Ship Canal Co. and Messrs. Crosfield. The latter claimed that the Canal Company were bound to dredge the bed of the river Mersey so that there should at all times be a depth of eight feet of water near Warrington. Mr. Cripps, K.C., and Mr. A. T. Lawrence appeared for the company, and asked for further time for lodging a cross appeal. Mr. Cripps stated that there were several extensions of time granted to the appellants,and they should have en extension also. Mr. Hughes, K.C. and, Mr. Frederick ThomsOn appeared for the appellants, Messrs. Crosfield and Sons. The Appeal Committee, Lord Halsbury and Lords Macnaghten, Davey, Robertson, and Atkinson, granted the extension of time, and allowed a cross appeal to be lodged.
